SAM MARKO PAVLOVICH
The Grand Master of Masons in California, Most Worshipful Sam Marko
Pavlovich, is a first generation American from California's Great Central
Valley. The son of immigrant Serbian parents who settled in Fresno after the
First World War', our Grand Master springs from solid, hardworking stock.
Raised with traditional Old World values of dedication to family, church, and
community, Sam Pavlovich has exemplified those qualities which have built
America.
Born in Fresno on February 1, 1921, Most Worshipful Brother Pavlovich
was raised in a family of five children: one brother and three sisters. After
attending high school in Fresno, our distinguished Brother studied engineering
at California State University, Fresno, but his studies were interrupted by the
Second World War, when he enlisted in the U.S. Navy. He served aboard a
destroyer escort in the European, African and Mediterranean theaters of war,
and while on active duty, was sent to th.e California Institute of Technology at
Pasadena, where he continued his studies until earning his honorable discharge
from the Navy.
Our distinguished Brother then completed a degree in general engineering
and became a registered civil engineer. He holds a certificate in transportation
planning from the University of California at Berkeley.
Most Worshipful Brother Pavlovich worked for the California State
Division of Highways and Cal-Trans for thirty-three years, retiring in 1981. His
district office was responsible for ~~Janning, design, construction and maintenance of the rapidly expanding · way system in the Central San Joaquin
Valley, including portions of U.S. 99 and Interstate 5.
Our Brother is an active member of the Serbian Orthodox Church, a part
of one of the major branches of historic Christianity. He served as Vice
President of St. Peter's Serbian Orthodox Church in Fresno when tbe present
building was built and subsequently for two terms as President of its Governing
Board. As a man of faith, he has exemplified the teachings of Orthodoxy in his
lifelong commitment to its principles.
In 1950, our Grand Master married the lovely Persida Kurilich, whose
parents had al.so come from Yugoslavia, from the Serbian Province of Hercegovina. They have three children -- Jo.Ann Kee~ Mark Pavlovich and Sandra
Vucovich -- and five grandchildren. Their daughter JoAnn was a member of the
Job' s Daughters and Mark was Master Councilor of his DeMolay Chapter.
A special highlight of his year as Grand Master was the special celebration
of the Fortieth Wedding Anniversary by our Grand Master and his lady, Persida.
The Grand Chaplain, the Very Reverend Robert Winterton, presided over a
Renewal of Wedding Vows by the couple at the Grand Master's Northern
Retreat in May, witnessed by the entire Grand Family.

SAM MARKO PAVLOVICH
Grand Master
October 11, 1989 - October 10, 1990

iii

Most Worshipful Brother Sam Pavlovich was raised to the Sublime Degree
of Master Mason in Las Palmas Lodge No. 366 on December 11, 1952. He
served as Master of that Lodge in 1967. A year later he was appointed Inspector
of the 416th Masonic District, a position he held for twelve years.
In 1980 he was appointed Assistant Grand Treasurer of the Grand Lod~e
of California, and then became a Trustee of the California Masonic Memonal
Temple in San Francisco. In 1986 he was elected Junior Grand Warden, and
progressed through the elective line until his election and installation as the
125th Grand Master of Masons in California. He was the first Grand Master to
serve as Grand Master of California alone, Hawaii having become a separate
Grand Jurisdiction when he was Deputy Grand Master.

I, ROBERT A . KLINGER, Grand Secretary of the M:. W:. Grand Lodge Free
and Accepted Masons of the State of California, do hereby certify tliat the
folio~ pages contain a true and faithful transcript of the proceedings of that
body at its One Hundred Forty-first Annual Communication, commencing at
the city of San Francisco, Monday the 8th day of October, A.L. 5990 and
terminating on Wednesday the 10th day of October, A.L. 5990.

Most Worshipful Brother Pavlovich has also been an active worker in other
vineyards in Freemasonry. He is a 33° Inspector General Honorary of the
Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, having been coroneted in 1981. He had
previously served as Master of Kadosh of the Fresno Consistory, and in 1980
was the Venerable Master of the Fresno Lodge of Perfection, also serving as
Secretary of all the Bodies from 1981 to 1988. He is a member of the Fresno
York Rite Bodies, and a member of the Allied Masonic Degrees and the Red
Cross of Constantine. He is also a member of the Royal Order of Scotland and
the National Sojourners.

of the State of California, at the office of the

in the year of Light, five thousand nine
hundred and ninety-one.

Other Masonic memberships include the Shrine, the Jesters, the Sciots and
the High Twelve. He is also a member of both the Central and the Southern
California Research Lodges. In addition, he has been invested with the
Honorary Legion of Honor by the Order of DeMolay, and, along with his wife
Persida, is a member of the Eastern Star and the Amaranth.

The One Hundred Forty-First Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California,
commenced at 9:00 a.m. on Monday, October 8, 1990, A.L. 5990, in the
California Masonic Memorial Temple located in San Francisco, California.
Prior to the opening of Grand Lodge, an Organ recital was presented by
Harold M . Hand, Grand Organist.
The opening session of the Annual Communication was raised by Bill M.
Ennis, Sr., Master of Las Palmas Lodge No. 366, the Lodge of the Grand Master,
and Hambleton Leas, a Past Master of that Lod~e. The gavel used to raise
Grand Lodge had been hand-crafted by C. Ray Whitaker, Grand Marshal, from
olive and birch from Grand Master Pavlovich's trees, and presented to him by
his grandchildren at Grand Lodge Installation in October, 1989.

formally received and presented at the Altar, after which the Brethren joined

Present during the Communication were 827 Officers and Representatives
from 528 chartered Lodges, 911 Past Masters, 215 Master Masons not members
of Grand Lodge and 30 Distinguished Guests from other Grand Jurisdictions.
Twenty-eight Grand Lodge Officers of this Jurisdiction as well as 19 Past Grand
Masters and 2 Past Grand Officers were registered. The total attendance was
2,032.

Devotional Message

Thousands of people stood in line for hours to see the exhibit called "The
City of Tomorrow". The huge, magnificently designed display, depicted buildings of glass and steel reaching far into the clouds; atop the buildings were
heliports. Moving sidewalks carried shoppers from store to store. The City was
custom designed to fulfill the needs of industry, education, services, protection
and recreation. Modern innovations were seen in every corner of the exhibit.
Two theological students approached one of the attendants with an incredulous observation, 'There does not seem to be any facility for worship in
the City of Tomorrow. In fact, there does not appear to be a single church,
mosque, synagogue or even a Lodge building where people might worship God."
The attendant at first seemed embarrassed, and then he proceeded with a
practiced cadence, "Well, sir, you see, the City of Tomorrow was not only
designed by architects and engineers, but sociologists and psychologists as well,
it was designed by them after carefully studying trends in society. They believed
there wouJd be no need for churches nor places of worship in the City of
Tomorrow."
My Brethren, this should come as no surprise to any of us given the changes
we have seen in the last decade alone, but you may find the rest of this story to
be startling indeed, when you learn that the exhibit called "The City of Tomorrow" took place at the Chicago World's Fair in 1914. There has always been, a
force in this would that would, if it could, destroy mankind's faith in a creator
God. That same force would have us abandon traditional values, and morality,
and replace them with situational ethics.
Indeed that force is powerful! We need look no farther than our own cities
and towns to see that immorality is rewarded and morality is punished. Convicted murderers freely walk the streets, rapists and mutilators of children are
slapped on the wrist and released to prey upon law-abiding citizens. Narcotics
sales vie with time-honored industries as the largest sources of revenue in our
country. There is scarcely a family left in America that bas not been touched by

the evils of elicit narcotics. The Masonic program for drug abuse education as
has been stated by Most Worshipful Sam Pavlovich, may be only a drop in the
bucket, but I pray to God that our half a million dollar drop will be added to by
millions more until the good men, called Masons, in California will have made
a dent in this vicious, Godless and immoral business. The force for evil in this
country1 by any name we car~ to call it, h<1:5 made alarming progress toward
destroying the home and family values. Which leads me to the purpose of this
dissertation. Brethren, since the inception of this great nation, Masons may have
disagreed on ritual, been confused about allegiances to Grand Lodges and we
may, in fact, now find ourselves in a dilemma as to which operational direction
Masonry will take in the last decade of this century...but we have never been
confused about common decency, morality and the value of the home. We have
embodied honesty, integrity and the virtues of free enterprise, separation of
<;hurcb and State and the freedoms of speech. and religion. For those prognosllcato.rs of.doom and gloom who would project the demise of Masonry, perhaps
even m this decade, allow me to propose that so long as there are Lodges of
Freemasons, we will defend the democratic rights of our great nation and we
will defend the rights of others to meet and worship in mosques, synagogues,
churches or other places of worship wherever they care to meet.
My Brethren, in this day of decadence and immorality, Freemasonry stands
as a tall tower of defense on behalf of the helpless. We are a wall and a fortress
against those who would freely disperse their venom of lawlessness, immorality
and atheism.
We are now met on this battlefield with a strange and mysterious counterforce! ~oun.d the world, in various and sundry places, organized religion has,
on occasion, 1den(tfied Freemasonry as an enemy of the church. Nothing could
be farther from the truth! Let me state loudly and clearly and without equivocation, "Freem~onry is not now, nor will it ever be~me, a religion! " Freemasonry
has no d<;>etnne. Freemasonry has no hymns, no liturgy, offers no salvation, nor
redempt10n, nor do we encompass the entire human race. We receive only men
21 years of age and older. We are not evangelical! Unfortunately, we cannot
even su~est to our closest friend or son, that he join our Fraternity. Masonry
does ask important questions about man's relationship with God. but answers
thos~ que~non~ in all~gory. Our Fraternity appeals to men who already have a
relallonship With therr Creator and those who simply believe that a Creator
e~sts. ~ost often those men, upon experiencing our Degrees, seek a closer walk
w:ith therr God through local churches. We are no enemy of the church! Most
Worshipful Sam Pavlovich has commissioned this Grand Chaplain and several
fo!'1Jler Grand Chaplains to prepare a paper on Masonry and religion. I am sorry
this paper could not be ready for distribution al this Communicauon of our great
Grand Lodge, but I promise you, and our Grand Master, that it will soon be
made available to all the Brethren of this jurisdiction in order that Masons
~ve~here may be fre.e to discuss .t he question of Masonry and religion in an
mtelligcnt and knowledgeable fashion.

In the meantime, my Brethren, we must be concerned with issues that face
us in these critical times. During the last decade of this century we will solve a
multitude of problems or leave our progeny with a quagmire in the next century.
First of all, we must realize that we are not simply an organization ...we are
an organism. We are a living, breathing voice compnsed of many members, each
with the unique and separate personality bound only by a common voluntary
obligation. We are not all the same! God has proven m ages past, and Masonry
continues to verify, that short men, tall men, fat men, skinny men, the educated
as well as the uneducated, men of every nationality are capable of speaking
eloquently throu~ this society called Freemasonry. We are at our best one-onone! Our ritual is 1D1pressive, our catechisms are well thought out and intelligent,
our social functions are pleasant. The Annual Commurucation of this Grand
Lodge sends shivers up and down my SJ?ine and causes goose bumps to pop out
on my flesh. When our Grand Orgarust, Worshipful Harold Hand, fills this
beautiful building with the organ's strains that signal the beginning of each
Communication, I am filled with wonder, awe and pride at be~ a part of this
great society, but Masonry never rises any higher than the relationship that is
almost instantaneously developed between two men when they realize their
common objectives. We must encourage these relationships.
I remember a story emanating from an opera hall in Paris. For months a
virtuoso baritone had been advertised in the lead of a prominent opera. On
opening night the festive crowd, dressed in their finest waited nervously for the
1
curtain to nse only to hear an announcement from the 1D1presario
that the noted
baritone had taken ill. Another baritone, a community artist, would perform the
lead. From the opening curtain it was obvious the crowd was disconsolate.
Although the local baritone's voice was more than ample for the task, it was met
with silence at the conclusion of every aria. The audience felt cheated and were
bound and determined to take out their wrath on the substitute star of the show.
The young baritone's voice attained beautiful clarity with the high notes and the
lowest register was solid, powerful and profound, but with the fmal notes of the
opera, the. crown remained silent. No one applauded! The silence was embarrassingly deafening! Finally, from the balcony, there arose a nine year old boy
and at the top of his lungs he yelled, "I think you're great, Daddy!" The boy's
exclamation was a spark that ignited the audience. As one, they rose in a
resounding, standing ovation. Tears flowed from the young baritone's eyes as
he answered curtain call after curtain call. The difference between success an.cl
failure in this particular instance was decided by a single person who possessed
the !lerve ~d the b_ravery to be first in expressing his appreciation. In this
particular instance, 1t was the performer's son. But perhaps any one person
could have turned the tide.
My Brethren, how often have we witnessed the accomplishments of one of
our Brothers go unheralded bec.ause no one was willing to go out on a limb and
say, "I think you're wonderful?" Often the wll$es of corn, wine and oil are
summed up in the single expression of appreciation by someone thoughtful
enough to express his inner feelings. We need to promote our Craft...what 6etter
way than to be a part of the paymaster's corps? Our Fraternity needs more

GRAND WOGE OF CALIFORNIA

9

supporters and fewer critics! If I were eloquent enough...if I had the ability to
sway this vast Communication of Masonic leaders, I would indelibly impress
upon your minds the importance of our Craft to our great nation. We love to
boast of our involvement in public libraries and public schools. Again and again
we count the great Masonic leaders who have impacted Am.e rican history. We
point with pride to Presidents, signers of the Declaration of Independence and
drafters of our Constitution. We speak of great moral victories forged by our
forefathers in the Craft, but we spend far too little time concentrating on the
fact that we are the only leaders Masonry has in 1990 and far too little time
dedicating ourselves to the significant tasks that lie before us in the last decade
of this important century. I believe that if we concentrated as much time on the
challenges of tomorrow, as we dedicate to guarding our Lodge savings accounts
today, we might just be reme.mbered by historians as the generation of Masons
who ignited the spark that revolutionized Freemasonry in America at the turn
of the century.
The task that lies before us is formidable. I mentioned, at the onset of this
Message, great enemies of morality that abound on every had. Those forces that
would negatively impact the moral fabric of America, have at their disposal not
only alcohol and drug abuse, not only latch-key children left to their own devices,
not only dishonesty and immorality in high political places, but my Brethren, I
believe those forces draw heavily on the nonchalance and apathy of modern
Masons. We must not be discouraged! We must persevere! We cannot afford
to give up. I am reminded of a young American musician who desir~ more
than anything else in the world, to l)ecome a great concert pianist. With the
backing of friends who believed in and supported him, be went from piano
teacher to piano teacher, each time being told he did not have the sharp, cutting,
competitive edge r~quired to master his chosen profession. He finally travelled
to Europe where ht. convinced a foremost piano teacher to take him as a student,
provided he worked eight hours a day at the keyboard. After a year, despite his
efforts, he was released by his teacher with words of discouragement and
despair. "You will never be a concert pianist," the instructor warned. "Your
fingers are not fast enough and in the quicker movements, you simply fake the
passage...you work hard at it, but you simply don't have the talent." Dejected,
the musician returned to America and tried his hand at several jobs but returned
again and again to the keyboard. He decided to perseveref What his piano
teachers overlooked while condemning his lack of talent was an ingredient
unknown at that time in the world of concert pianists ... showmanship! I
know...you think you know the pianist. No, my Brethren, he was not Liberace,
he was Paderewskil When I heard this story of perseverance as told by Paul
Harvey on "The Rest of the Story", I was surprised that Paul Harvey didn't know
the rest of the story. Years later, in a concert hall in New York, a gathering
~rowd breathlessly awaited the appearance of the great Paderewski. Dressed
m tuxedos and evening dresses, the crowd did not notice the six year old boy
who, having seen the beautiful black Steinway concert piano on the stage, and
no one to play it, somehow escaped his mother's critical eye, ascended the stage
an.d was seating himsel!' at the keys. The child's hands began to play the only
thing be knew... Chopsticks! The huge crowd was aghast! His mother undoubtedly was unwilling to claim him. The great Paderewski, waiting off stage,

grasped the situation in a second, strode from the wings and without any
announcem ent, leaned over and whispered in the little boy's ear, "Keep going,
don't stop. Keep playing, don't stop." And then with his own talented right hand,
be began playing a counter melody on the treble keys. With the little boy as a
centerpiec e, be composed a counter melody to Chopsticks that would be the
stock in trade of Eddie_l?ucbjn, Carm~n Cavallero and Liber~ce. He kept time
by the constant admomtton , Keep gomg, don't stop, keef gomg, don't stop." I
would admonish you, my Brothers, that in the face o opposition...dcspite
~couragement ~d lack of suppo~ keep ~oing, don't stop. I am told that
WUlSton Churchill spent four years m the eighth grade because he couldn't
master the English language. After an illustrious career that made him the most
famous name in the world during the Second World War, he was invited to
lecture the graduating class at OX:ford University. Upon being introduced , he
s~rode across the stage to the lectern wearing his famous Homburg hat, carrying
his cane and smoking a cigar. He stopped, r emoved his hat, laid his cigar upon
the rostrum and scanned the huge open air amphithea ter, then pronounce d in
a booming voice, "Never give up!" He rose on his toes, again surveyed the crowd
and proclaimed in his loudest voice, "Never give up. !" He thc.n placed his hat on
his head, stuck his cigar firmly in his teeth and strode from the platform to a
rousing ovation. He was finished with his speech.
l suspect that in the next twelve months many of you will want to give. up.
Many of you having donned the top hat of Master of your Lod~e will discover
that there is as much opposition to your plans and aspirations within the Lodge
as there is from without. Some of you will discover Secretarie s who will wrestle
you for the gavel. Still other members will be militant defenders of the status
quo and spokesmen for mediocrity. You may want to give up, but don't!
Across the length and breadth of this great nation the decline in moral

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

My Brethren:
One year ago, embarking upon the awesome duties of the office of Grand
Master, with a deef sense of appreciation and with utmost humility, I alluded
to the magnitude o : the task before me. l accepted that responsibility and then
a feeling of inadequacy descended upon me as the Installation Ceremony
concluded and the customary proclamation was made by the Grand Marshal.
Only then did I truly realize the magnitude of the work to be done and that of
my own shortcomings as the weight of responsibilities to come dropped upon
my shoulders. My fervent hope and prayers were that I would be found worthy
of that trust reposed in me.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

29

unbelievable rapidity. The Great Architect has been good to me in granting

g<_>O<l health, and the support and understanding of my loved ones during purswt
of my Masonic endeavors.

In moments of solitude, I often-times reflect as to the other alternatives in
my life style had my parents opted not to ~grate to this, µi~ gre.atcst country
on the face oF the p~anet e":fth. The .opporturuty aa:orde~ ~ rmmigrant farmer
and his wife is manifested m the ability to rear their family m an atmosphe~e of
freedom and happiness in a n~wly adopte~ ho.m eland. Their ~ome has provtded
the environment, the foundatt~n, the family ~fe style, an~ with sm~e of.the old
world traditions, generated basic moral teachings and desired qualifications for
acceptance of their two sons int<? the ~asonic Fraternity. AnC?th~r examp!e of
opportunity in action and the umversality of our great Fratermty is personified
in the substance and character of the Grand Master now before you. Where else
except under these extraordinary conditions could the son of an immigrant .be
bestowed with the greatest of gifts from the Brethren of his beloved Califorrua?
For all these things I shall be ever grateful!
And now that my stewardship is approaching its closing moments, I vividly
recollect the admonition given to me during the Installation Ceremony one year
ago; namely that I was only first among myJeers. I realized then as I do now
that I would so soon be reduced and returne to the ranks of my colleagues but,
in all reality, I hope that I never left or rose above them.
We have all witnessed with awe and admiration the carefully orchestrated
V-formations of geese in their migration. The leader instinctively breaks the
barrier of wind force for the geese on his left and right. Knowing this, most
people naturally as6Ume the geese choose the strongest and most experienced
as their leader. Such, however, is not the case. As the lead goose tires, he drops
back and another takes his (>lace. But the old leader doesn't drop out of the
formation; he simply joins it m the rear, often to lead again. Similarly, we must
prepare ourselves to be replaced by younger Brothers with new visions, new
dreams and steadfast determination. But we still must persist. We must stay in
the formation. Akin to this story is the comforting thought that hopefully in my
retirement, I shall remain in the ranks, fly in the formation and possibly in some
humble capacity contribute to the work and welfare of this Grand Lodge and
our great Fraternity.

It bas been a long-established custom of this Grand Lodge, as well as "the
duty of the Grand Master, to present, at each Annual Communication, a written
message, therein setting forth all his official acts during the year, exhibiting the
general condition of Masonry within the Jurisdiction, and recommending such
legislation as he may deem necessary or expedient for the welfare of the Craft".

The past year truly has been a busy one for the Grand Lodge family. With
19 - Cornerstones, 2 - Public School Dedications, 1 - Constitution, 1 - Mortgage
Burning, 7 - Seventy-five Year Pin Ceremonies, 42 - Receptions, 2 - Outdoor
Third Degrees, and numerous other events, we have been mobile. The itinerary
attached to this Message speaks to the ~eographic extent of our travels and to
the numerous events in which we participated.

I now stand before you, with humble heart, accountable as you deliberate
on how successfully I have utilized the golden opportunity that was given to me,
or how ineffectually I may have administered your affairs. My judge and jury, it
seems but yesterday, that I stood before you and yet the year has come and gone.
The days and weeks and months have succeeded each other with almost

The opportunity to meet, greet and clasp the hands of Brethren throughout
our jurisdiction and the ability to share in fraternal fellowship, truly were Master
Mason's wages for this Grand Master. My desire to bring "Grand Lodge" to our
masses and thus to accord those who rarely meet an officer of Grand Lodge the

State of the Craft
May I convey to you the information which I know can never be appreciated
except by those who have actually discharged the duties of this office. I have
literally traveled the length and breadth of our Golden State on numerous
occasions and have crisscrossed our commonwealth from her blue Pacific
shores to the beautiful Sierras. In so doing, I have been gratified to find on my
many visitations to Lodges and Masonic Districts that the Fraternity seems to
be strong and healthy notwithstanding the distressing membership reversals
which have been in our midst for quite some time. Lodges which appear to be
flourishing are those with planned activities and resultant good attendance
whereas many others are floundering and barely struggle to stay in existence.
Consolidations are on-going. The 1989-90 Masonic Year has witnessed
eleven consolidations with two additional merging activities in progress at the
time of this printing. This will result in a net decrease of U Lodges this year.
Inspectors' reports mdicate no relief in sight as numerous other consolidations
are under consideration for the next Grand Lodge year. Our avera~e age
continues to be on the rise and stands at more than 65. Deaths, dinuts and
suspensions for non-rayment of dues far exceed the number that we are raising.
As a consequence o this statistic our membership during 1990 bas suffered a
net loss of 5,717 and stands at 145,312 as of June 30, 1990. Entered Apprentices
and Fellow Crafts are being dropl'ed at an alarming rate. We must review this
statistic and our law relating to it m order to prevent the continued loss of this
most precious comm.o dity. A more detailed analysis of membership statistics
will be found in the Grand Secretary's report elsewhere in these Proceedings.

In spite of the foregoing, the spirit of Masonry seems to be alive and active
in all. the Lodges visited, notwithstanding these indicators of doom and gloom,
I am convinced that Freemasonry remains on top of the heap as the best
Fraternity in the world! However, I have other concerns, concern that this
Fraternity of ours is being judged -- not by reason of the accuracy of any design
upon the Trestleboard; not by the correctness of any ritual or ceremony; not by
the buttons which we wear on our lapels; and not by any names on a rosler or
d~llars in a treasury, but only by the success which we attain in ma.king these
things meaningful in the lives of the membership of this order. The communities

in which we live must be better and richer because of the truths which we teach.
The success of Masonry does not depend totally upon the numbers we initiate,
but it does depend upo n whether the lessons we communicat e to these members, the prece pts we publish to the world, are making for better citizens and
better citizenship in the communities in which they live.

Dedsloo No. 3
At its 1990 Annual Commu nication , the Grand Lodge of Washing to n,
following the lead of the Grand Lodges of Connect icut and Nebrask a, and later
followed by Wiscons in and perhaps others, granted recognit ion to the regulari
of the Ponce Hall Grand Lodge of Washin gton and extende d visitatioty
privileges to Prince Hall Masons , to its constitu ent Lodges, and to its Grandn

Lodge.

The Grand Lddge of Californ ia has not recogniz ed the resulari ty of any
Prince Hall Grand Lodge in any state in the United States, including Californ
ia,
for the reason that our America n Doctrin e of Exclusive Territor ial Jurisdic tion
as enuncia ted in Section 7(b) of our California Masonic Code prohibit s us from
doing so. That Doctrin e permits us to recognize only one Masonic Grand Lodge
in any state or territory and further provides that the Grand Lodge recogniz ed
by us has exclusive control and governm ent of all Masons and all Lodges of the
three degrees within that state or territory.
Because of our law, several of our California Masons who reside in the State
of Washingt_on, or who have affiliated with Washing ton Lod~es, question
ed
wbethe.r therr attendan ce in consti~uent Lodges un<fer the junsdict ion of the
recognized Grand Lodge of Washington, exposed them to Masonic charges
under our law due to the possibility ofsitting in Lodge with individuals who are
m~mbers of Lodges under the junsdict ion of Grand Lodges no t recogniz
ed by
this Grand Lodge.
Section 2032 of our Californ ia M asonic Code forbids us from admittin g into
our Lodges any person who is not acknowledged as a Mason by this Grand
Lodge and further forbids us from holding Masonic intercou rse with any such
person anywhere in the world.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

38

At the same time, however, Section 2610 of our Code allows us to act in
accordance with the law, policy and J?ractice of another Masonic jurisdiction
recognized by California when within that jurisdiction. Since the Masonic
Grand Lodge of Washington recognizes as Masonic, persons not considered as
Masons by this Grand Lodge, these two conflicting Sections of our Code must
be balanced and resolved
I have concluded that any Grand Lodge in any state or territory of the
United States currently recognized by the Grand Lodge of California which
reco~izes any o.ther Grand 1:-<'dge o~ M~ons ~ i~s jurisdicti~n, violates the
American Doctnne of Exclusive Terntonal Junsdicllon to which we adhere.
Nevertheless1 I have also determined that each Grand Lodge recognized by us
has original legislative, judicial and executive power over all Masons and all
~ge.s within its r.espective jurisdictio~ ai;id .th~t ~o. other Grand Lodge,
mcluding ours, may 10 any way mterfere with its Jurisdiction. Consequently, the
determination by any Grand Lodge to recognize a Grand Lodge not recognized
by us is within its exclusive control and government, and the fact that we believe
that they may be in violation of even their own law as to exclusive territorial
jurisdiction is not cause for California to withdraw recognition and thus forbid
fraternal relations among the members of our two Grand Lodges.
It is therefore my Decision that so long as the Grand Lodge of California
continues to recognize a particular Grand Lodge, members of California
Lodges residing in or visiting or affiliating with Lodges under the jurisdiction
of that Grand Lodge may sit in those Lodges with persons reco~d as Masons
by those Jurisdictions although not so recognized by California. Our members
may not visit or affiliate with constituent Lodges of any Grand Lodge not
~ecognized by the Grand Lodge of California nor may they hold Masonic
mtercourse with any member of any unrecognized Grand Lodge or of its
C?nstituent Lodges except that Masonic intercourse with a person not recogruzed as a Mason by this Grand Lodge shall be permitted when sitting in Lodges
or appendant organizations under the jurisdiction of Grand Lodges recognized
by the Grand Lodge of California, provided that such person is recognized as
a Mason by those Grand Lodges.
Nothing in this Decision shall authorize a California Mason to vouch for
any ~e!Dber of any ~e~gnized Grand Lodge or ~ts constituent Lodges to ~ain
admiss10n to a California Lodge as would otherwise be permitted by Sections
2416 and 2418 of the California Masonic Code.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

. Notwithsta~ding the generosity of Broth~r Tate and the Na.tional Fo~da­
llon, I was reqwred to decide that our Masoruc law -- more specificaUy California Masonic Code Section 2305 -- will not permit our Temple Associations to
engage in any activities not in furtherance of their exclusive purpose to hold title
to property, collect income therefrom and turn over the entire amount thereof,
less expenses, to its members or shareholders.
The suggestion was then made that the fund be distributed to Seafaring
Masonic Lodge No. 708 as Trustee of a separate fund irrevocably dedicated to
charitable p~ses so as to qualify under Internal Revenue Code Section
501(c)(3).Agam it was necessary to look at our law and to the policy and general
purposes of the fraternal orgaruzation of our Lodges to determine whether or
not this would be permissible.
Although Trust funds are not truly "Lodge funds" as they are held by the
Trustee exclusively to carry out the purpose of the Trust, I found it necessary
to conclude that it is the S{>irit of our law and policy for our Lodges to engage
solely in the Masonic actiVtties of initiating, passing and raising candidates and
using their funds for strictly Masonic purposes as more specifically set forth in
Secttons 2300 through 2322 of the California Masonic Code. Likewise, I concluded that although Lodges may accept donated funds in trust under California
Masonic Code Section 2316 "for any proper pur,P?se", use of those funds outside
of the Fraternity for other than Masoruc actiVIties would not be for a "proper
purpose" as contemplated by Section 2316 and would be contrary to our policy
and law.
It was my duty, therefore, to conclude that our law is clear -- particularly as
we read California Masonic Code Sections 2300(a) and 2316(m)-- that a Lodge
may not establish a foundation with power to administer, hold, invest and
reinvest funds as may be received by it from gift~ bequests, grants, contributions
or otherwise; and, because charity outside or the Fraternity is not a lawful
purpose for Lodge funds.
Notwithstanding the foregoing, I am very pleased to report that with the
full cooperation of Seafaring Masonic Lodge No. 708, its Building Association
and legal. counsel, and through the unde~slanding and generosity ~f the He.r man
Tate Urutrust II Trustees and the Nallonal Foundation for Philanthropy, we
were able to agree that the funds could be distributed to the California Masonic
Foundation, a charitable corporation which has qualified under Section
501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code, and deposited into a separate fund.
Seafaring Lodge shaU appoint a Committee to recommend to the Masonic
F?undatio~ org~tions to wbfc~ the incon:ie and principal shaU be distnbuted, with credit from the recipients to be given to Seafarmg Lodge.
I also am greatly pleased to report to you that the Masonic Homes of
California is named to receive an amount equal to the Seafaring Lodge fund for
its use through its general fund.

41

Therefore, it is my Decision that:
1. A Masonic Temple Association may not hold or administer
funds for any purpose not specifically set forth in California
Masonic Code Section 2305; and
2. The words "any proper purpose" as set forth in the first
paragraph of Section 2316 are construed to mean "any proper
Masonic purpose", and the administration of funds by a Lodge
for purposes other than those referred to in Sections 2.100
through 2322 is not permitted.

During the term that I have served as your Grand Master, I have been

that although our law does not specificaUy prohibit Grand Lodge from undertaking such activities, our constituent Lodges and appendant organizations are
forbidden to do so.

Decision No. 7
I have been requested by several Brothers to interpret the ~alifornia
Masonic Code with respect to the placement of the Candidate's chair. for the
lectures and proficiencies in the Three Degrees. In 1987, the Committee on
Ritual changed the positioning of the Candidate's chair from its "traditional
position" between the Worshipful Master and the Altar lo a place between the
Altar and the Senior Warden. I am informed that the reasoning for doing this
was:
1. That the vision of the Master be not obstructed to the Three
Great Lights; and
2. The Master should be required to project his voice
throughout the Lodge Hall rather than limit it to the Candidate alone.

I do not fault the reasoning of the Ritual Committee and certainly it is
entitled to use reasonable di.c;cretion in supervising the teaching of the Ritual in
a manner that will best carry out its charge, provided that it does not change the
Ritual as prohibited by Section 2690 of the California Masonic Code. The
relocation of the Candidate's chair for the purpose of lectures is not, in °:fu:ew,
a change in the Ritual and, for this reason, I have concluded that it is wi · the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

43

province of the Ritual Committee to determine the placement of the Candidate
for the lectures.
However, the positioning of the Candidate's chair for examination as to
proficiency is specifically governed by our law in that Section 2668 of the
California Masonic Code states in pertinent part, that the examination of the
Candidate" . . . shall be held in front of the East". As a result, the discretion of
the Ritual Committee is restricted to cause such examination to be held in front
of the East. It, therefore, became my duty to interpret the meaning of those
words "in front of the East".
Nowhere does our law define the specific location of the East, West or
South. For example, is the East the entire area from the center of the Altar to
the wall behind the Master and is the West the entire are from the center of the
Altar to the area behind the Senior Warden? If we conclude those definitions
to be accurate, then we have to determine the location of the South. ls that from
a point bisecting the Altar in the opposite direction running east and west the
entire length of the Lodge Hall to an area behind the Junior Warden?
We often refer to the East as being a specific place such as the chair of the
Worshipful Master and like definitions are given for the West being the station
of the Senior Warden and the South being the station of the Junior Warden.

As you can see, it is easy to get cau£ht up in the semantics of this language
when words of the law seem so slDlple. We traced the legislative history of the
specific wording in Section 2668 and found that the ~age was added in 1922
but, unfortunately, no reasons were given and no specific location was defined
for "in front of the East".
I do not dispute that the relocation of the Candidate's chair is technically
in front of the East. That is to say it is not behind the East, or for that matter,
to the side of the East. Nevertheless, legislative construction requires that
reasonable meaning be given to words and I have concluded that the relocation
of the Candidate's chair was to a position in front of the Altar and not in front
of the East.
Notwithstanding my conclusion, our Lodge rooms differ substantially in

~eir confi~ation and our Ritual Co~ttee must be given reasonable leeway

m C?';lfornung the floor work to various Lodge rooms. It is therefore my
Dee1S1on that the sentence in Section 2668 .in the California Masonic Code
reading:
"Such examination shall be held in front of the East"
means that the examination must be conducted in an area in front of the Master

~din a location between the Altar and the Master's chair. The specific location

will be within the discretion of the Committee on Ritual to determine.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master's Decision No. 2 concerns the rules approved by the 1989
Grand Lodge to provide for a situation where similar, but conflicting, measures
are both adopted as law. These rules were accepted by the Grand Lodge without
objections, and before the ballot was taken.
The rules in question were taken from the California Constitution, Article
2, Section lO(b), which reads as follows: "U provisions of two or more measures
approved at the same election conflict, those of the measure receiving the
highest affirmative vote shall prevail".
Such rules are essential to the safeguard of the integrity of our balloting
process. Sections 502 and 4002 of the California Masonic Code state in part; "if
five-sixths of the votes shall be in favor of such proposed amendment it shall be
declared adopted". In 1989 two issues of a similar but conflicting nature were
considered. Both received a proper affirmative vote. Grand Master Channon's
Recommendation No. 12 received 1,462 affirmative votes, whereas Carry-over
Resolution No. 88-19 received 1 304. According~. wherever a conflict arose in
the two matters the language o Recommendation No. 12 prevailed. Also, in
accordance with the democratic process and the rules approved by the 1989
Grand Lodge, the non-conflicting portions of Carry-over Resolution No. 88-19
became at once a separate amendment and was likewise adopted.

1

The contrary argument of "the winner take all" is not valid in that both
proposals were "winners" in their own right. It is true that one proposal received
1,462 votes while the other received 1,304. It should be pointed out, however,
that the two issues were not considered simultaneously, but rather with a
considerable time difference. Those of us who arc privileged to view the Grand
LOOse from the platform can see its makeup fluctuate almost hourly with
parncula.r emphasis on certain times of the day.
. .My.Brethren, a legitimate majority vote of this Grand Lodge, on a non-conffictmg ISsue, sho uld not and must not ever be disfranchised.
We agree with the language set forth by the Code Commission in Section
204~ ?f the California Masoruc Code, and we support the Grand Master's
Decis10n to apply Article 2, Section lO(b) to the California Constitution as a

proper and reasonable accommodation to the expressed intent of the Grand
Lodge.
We recommend a "Yes" vote.

DECISION NO. S
ADMINJSTRATION OF TRUST FUNDS BY LODGES

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Grand Master's Decision No.
5 has been referred, reports as follows:
The Grand Master has determined that there exists no authority in Sections
2300 through 2322 of our California Masonic Code, or elsewhere in the law, for
Masonic Lodges, or Masonic Temple Associations to hold or administer trust
funds or other funds for any purpose other than those specifically referred to
in said Sections 2300 through 2322 and that the term, "any proper purpose", as
used in Section 2316 of the Code means, "any proper Masonic purpose".
Your Committee finds that this Decision is consistent with our law and does
not require an amendment to the California Masonic Code. As a result, only a
majority affirmative vote is required for approval.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Pavlovich found it necessary in his Decision No. 5 to determine whether or not it was proper for a Masonic Temple Association or
Masonic Lod$e to hold funds, not its own, in trust for irrevocably dedicated
purposes. In his Decision, the Grand Master concluded that not only as a matter
of law but policy as well it is not proper. He further concluded that that portion
of Section 2316 of the California Masonic Code which states, "except that where
funds are donated and accepted in trust for any proper purpose they may be
used for it", shall be construed as "any proper Masonic purpose". The Commit-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNJA

55

tee on Policy and General Purposes agrees with the Grand Master on both
counts.
We find nothing under the policy practices, or procedures, of this Grand
Lodge that would permit a Lodge to hold and manage funds other than its own
to be used for outside charitable purposes, no matter how worthy they m~y be.
To the contrary, we find it to go well beyond the "general purposes" of California
freemasonry. In 1936, Grand Master Warren was asked, in two separate issues,
as to wbe~~r it.was proper for t~e Trustees of a Masonic Lodge.to receive funds
and secunttes m trust for certaio purposes, namely to the ultunate benefit of
members of the donor Mason's family. Grand Master Warren answered as
follows: "Nowhere does the Constitution or Masonic law ex,pressly authorize
trustees of a Lodge to act as trustees for individual brethren . It should follow
then that it would likewise be improper to hold funds in trust outside the
Masonic family. California Masonic law in Section 2300a prohibits the establishment of a foundation, by a Lodge, for certain charitable or beneficent
purposes. We find little difference between such foundation and the proposed
trust fund, except in name.
The.Grand Master's construction of Section 2316 of the California Masonic
Code to mean "for any proper Masonic purpose" is likewise in concert with the
opinion of Lhis Committee. The funds alluded to under that Section have long
been permitted when donated to a Lodge, in trust for a specific purpose. The
funds so donated become at once the property of the Lodge to be used for a
designated purpose. Such purposes include, but are not limited to, a Lodge
buildin~ fund, a Lodge maintenance fund, purchase of a Lodge organ, all proper
Masomc purposes.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes• vote
on Grand Master's Decision No. 5.

This Committee has some very strong policy opinions regarding the "traditional" placement of the chairs, however, this report will not deal with those
opinions, but will be limited to the reasoning behind the Grand Master's two
part Decision.
Section 2668 of the California Masonic Code deals with the requirements
for the proficiency examinations in the Apprentice and Fellow Craft Degrees.
The Grand Master's Decision is limited to the last sentence of the Section which
reads as follows: "Such examination shall be held in front of the East". It was
concluded by the Grand Master that such language be constructed as that area
between the Altai •II ! the Master's chair. We agree with the Grand Master.
. I! has long been the custom of Cra~ Lodges to re~ard the Al~ar as the "f~l
pomt of the Lod~e room, or more specifically the pomt from which all Masoruc
light and inst.ruction emanates. It, therefore, must be recognized as a delineation
point for the several parts of the compass alluded to in the Degrees. It likewise
establishes itself as a barrier, or point of demarcation for the stations in the
Lodge room. When a Candidate is conducted from one geographic representation in the Lodge to another, he is taken by a pre-determmed route around
the Altar as it would not be possible to pass through it. The words "in front or
must have a definitive mearung. We submit to you, my brethren, that if it were
announced that some one of you should meet another person "in front of the
Grand Lodge building" at the end of today's session, you sho uld not be expected
to look for that person on the steps of the Grace Cathedral across the street.
The Grand Master's wisdom should prevail in his ruling that the
Candidate's examination must be given between the Altar and the Master's
chair, as a matter of law, and cannot be superceded by ritualistic discretion.
The Grand Master also ruled correctly that the relocation of the chair for
the lectures is not a change in the ritual and therefore is within the reasonable
discretion of the Ritual Committee.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes urgc.s a "Yes" vote on
Grand Master's Decision No. 7.

The Committee on Ritual:

The Grand Master bas recommended that, because of the unique
geographical scope of the Shrine East-West Footb~ Game an~ its c~a~er
as a maJor and important annual event solely benefit:.Ulg a M~~°:1c org~1;1on
sponsored charity, the Game be exempted from our law prohib1tmg adverusmg,
provided that the advertising meets reasonable standards.

We have struwed to find some vivid and impressive way to express to you
the importance ofYour vote on th.is Recommendation. All of our efforts have
fallen short of the mark. To put it simply, th.is may be the most important vote
you've ever cast. You've had important issues before you every year, and th.is
year is no exception, but nothing has struck so critically at the heart, the very
soul, of Masonry. Unless you support th.is Recommendation by the Grand
Master, Masonry, as we know it, very possibly will not survive.
Resolution No. 88-17, which was passed last year, limits an Inspector to no
more than nine consecutive years in that position. What no one knew when we
voted was that the rule would apply retroactively. That interpretation was
explained only after the vote was cast. The result is that 35 Inspectors must be
replaced at the end of~ year. That's nearly one qu¥ler of the Inspectoral
Corps, gone at the same bme. Remember also, more will have to go at the end
of next year, and more every year after that. In addition, normal resignations
will cause still more vacancies.
It's acknowledged that even the most competent rituaJist will need three or
four years to become a skilled Inspector. This learning curve, coupled with the
mandated turnover, means that in three or four years, 60 to 70 percent of the
Inspectors will be new. To look at it another way, 60 to 70 percent of our Lodges,
60 to 70 percent of our Officers, will have to look to new Inspectors for
instruction and guidance.

In Resolution No. 90-12, the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens call our
ritual "our most important possession." Masonic scholars have long said that it
is our ritual which distinguishes us from all other fraternities. Do you truly want
to support legislation which would cause 2/3 of our Inspectors, those invested
with the responsibility to teach "our most important possession", to be less than
adequately prepared?
By your vote on th.is Recommendation, you will decide the fate of our ritual.
You will decide if it is to survive or perish. We ask that you respect our Grand
Master's perspective and heed his sound advise. We urge your "Yes" vote.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

We have been deeply concerned, in recent years with the time constraints
placed upon the delegates of this Grand Lodge as they attempt to express their
views on the several issues being considered. We agree that an "open
microphone" policy will be abused on occasion, however, we believe a restriction
on reasonable debate to be far more de trimental to the proceedings of this
Grand Lodge than the abuse or privilege. My Brethren, we must remember that
we ~ther here on these occasions for one purpose, and that is to conduct the
bUSlDess of this Grand Lodge. If it is important enough to be considered at all
then we should allot the necessary time to do so.
It has been suggested that we go back to the four day format for our Annual
Communication. This would certainly provide the additional time needed for
the conduct of business, but with the additional ?Ost of one day, in excess of fifty
thousand dollars, the Grand Master's suggestton may be the more prudent
solution to the dilemma.
A Sunday afternoon opening could accommodate all of the pomp and
ceremony of opening the Grand LodBe, the recognition of our Past Grand
Masters, the esc-0rt of our visiting dignitaries and the recognition of the representatives of our concordant and appendant organiz.ations. We could then roll
up our sleeves on Monday morning and go to work on the business of this Grand
Lodge.
With the admonition that you are not voting today to change the o~ning
day of Grand Lodge, rather to appoint a Comrmttee to study tlie feasibility of
the same, we call for your "Yes" vote.

The Committee on Finance:
It has been the position of your Finance Committee for several years that
the ever increasing costs of the Annual Communication and Grand Lodge Week
Activities needed to be given very serious review and study.
It should be noted that the Annual Communication activities are not only
attended by a small percentage of the registered delegates but those who do
attend are being subsidized by ever increasing amounts every year.
The Deputy Grand Master has indicated, if approved, he will appoint from
3 to 5 members to this Special Committee and that the Committee will hold
approximately three meetings.
Your Finance Committee is of the opinion that the expenses for this
Committee should not exceed $5,000 in the coming fiscal year.
Since one of the directives to the Committee will be to study our Annual
Communication costs, it may be that as a result of their deliberations an overall
reduction in Grand Lodge expenses may be achieved.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

67

At this time, however, your Committee on Finance has no way of estimating
the extent of any reduction in expenses.
Your Committee on Finance recommends a "Yes" vote on Grand Master's
Recommendation No. 3.
Recommendation ADOPTED.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Grand Master and Senior Grand Warden express a commendable
desire to promote the visibility of Freemasonry to the pi.iblic via the proposed
float.
While it is estimated that more than one million persons will view the parade
in person, and another 57 million will see the parade on television, there is a
question as to how many of the non-Masonic viewers would comprehend the
meaning of Freemasonry and the theme of the float. Of the total of about 58
million viewers, non-Masons would make up approximately 98.7 {>ercent. Also,
the exposure of the float to these viewers would last only a few nunutes at best,
and would not have the benefit of repetition as with commercial television
advertising.
However, the Grand Lodge did sponsor such a float several years ago with
the similar desire of promoting Freemasonry to the public. To the best of our
knowledge, relatively few of those who viewed the float, eventually became
members of the Fraternity, or expressed new interest in the Fraternity.

This Committee did support that project, it being the 200th Anniversary of
our Nation.
While it would help the expense of the pr~am if other Masonic Jurisdictions in the United States would participate pnor to our Grand Lodge having
committed itself, there is no evidence of such participation.

RECOMMENDATION NO. S
PROCEDURES FOR BALLOTING UPON CONSOLIDATION.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Grand Master's Recommendation No. 5 has been referred, reports as follows:

With the continuing decline in membership, and the continuing increases
in costs of operation, it is likely that the Finance Committee will find it necessary
to recommend an increase in the annual per-capita tax without consideration
being ~ven to the proposed float project. Constituent Lodges also fee the effects
of similar financial pressure in their operations.

The Grand Master has recommended that certain procedures be followed
by Lodges in balloting upon consolidations.

In recent years this Gr and Lodge has made it possible for individual Lodges
to promote Masonry's visibility in their local communities by permitting booths
to be established at the State and County Fairs where those manning the booths
could promote public relations.

RESOLVED, that Section 2104 of the California Masonic Code be
amended by adding the following paragraph thereto;

Also, Lodges are permitted to sell food and non-alcoholic beverages at
community events. Not only does such Lodge earticipation represent potential
income to the Lodge, but it furthers Lodge visibility and public relations in the
community.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes commends the Grand
Master, the Senior Grand Warden and the Ad Hoc Committee from Van Nuys
Lodge for their intent. We believe that the cost of the project and the uncertainty
of our National economics suggest that this is not the time for the Grand Lodge
to commit itself to a project of this magnitude.
Therefore, we recommend a "No" vote.

To carry out the intent of the Grand Master, your Committee on
Jurisprudence submits the following Resolution:

"T~e f<;>llowing procedures shall be followed in balloting upon consolidauons:

1. The ballot solicited from the members of a Lodge shall be
accompanied by a fair and impartial fact sheet setting forth all
relevant information reasonably necessary to enable the members to vote intelligently. No other written material concerning
the proposed consolidation shall be sent to the members by
anyone except as hereafter set forth.
2. No ~tte!l ma.terial accomp~ying any ballot shall contain
any solic1tal1on either for or agrunst a proposed consolidation.

3. The members shall be directed by the Master to re~n lheir

selected by the Master.
4. No envelope containing.a ballot 1n:ay be opened by ~yone
prior to the Stated Meetmg at which such ballots ~ be

final and binding upon the ~e and no further ballot shall

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master's Recommendation No. 5 has grown out of his Decision
. olidation procedures taken by Parnass~-Presidio ~~e
No. 4 relating to cons
No. 388 and Columbia-Balder Lodge No. 393. Th~ appli~ble California
Masonic Code Section 2104 does not now set forth specific dt:tailed pr~ures
for obtaining consent form:; from members of Lodges attemptmg to consolidate.
Because of the immediate unusual necessities of the above noted case, the
Grand Master issued the procedural steps set out in his Recommendation No.
5. He recommends now that they~ ~dopted as part of our Ordinances made
applicable to future Lodge consolidations as well.
Our Committee believes that experience has shown that most Lodge C?Dsolidations experience only the normal amount of "bumps and sputters" dunng
completion of the unification process under present law, an~ th.at to regulate
each detail to be followed under 2104 for all future c:nns?lidal!ons co~d 1?e
overly burdensome for Lodges already in need of consolidation help to mamtam
strength.

GRANDLODGEOFCALWORNIA

71

We believe the instructions issued by the Grand Master on the particular
problem at hand were appropriate and helpful. However, it has long been the
position of our Committee to avoid recommending that our Ordinances be
changed to affect all Lodges based upon problems arising from a single case.
To make a detailed processing procedure which is applicable for an unusual
situation the required standard ofprocedure for all future consolidations would
be unnecessary and impractical.
In addition to q_uestioning the need for these new proceedings, we have a
specific concern with the content of on.e of them. The Recommendation
prohibits any member of the Lodge from mailing anything to the membership
to argue either in favor of or in opposition to the proposed consolidation. While
such argument could take the place at a Stated Meeting, the decision will be
made by the entire membership, not just th.at small percentage in attendance at
the Stated Meeting. The prohibition against contacting those other members in
writing denies a proponent or opponent any effective means of pleading his case
to the ultimate decision makers. Thus, this procedure impairs, rather than
promotes, the right of a member to be heard on this vital issue.

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
Recommendation NOT ADOPTED.

The report and comments of the Grand Treasurer are based on the official
statements of Lindquist, von Husen and Joyce, Certfied Public Accountants , of
San Francisco, whose reports are an inte~al part of the Grand Treasurer's
Report. Their audit covers the year ending June 30, 1990, and contains a
complete record of income and expenses for the period.

As I have reminded in previous reports, you, the delesates to the Annual
Communication, are, in effect, the stockholders of the entities of Grand Lodge
and your reading and comments to the reports is recommende d and encouraged.
While governments may operate with a fiscal deficit, the organization s
which constitute the total Grand Lodge family conduct their business under
budgetary controls which keep income and expenses in proper balance. The
assets and investments of our Masonic entities are well managed and protected.
We are grateful to the members of the Masonic Fraternity in California who
are noted for their ~enerosity which is reflected in contribution s to the Masonic
Homes of Califorma,an d the California Masonic Foundation. We have had the
complete cooperation of Most Worshipful Sam M. Pavlovich and his Officers,
that of Grand Secretary Robert A. Klinger, the Trustees of the Masonic Homes,
California Masonic Memorial Temple and the California Masonic Foundation.
And I wish to especially thank the Accounting staff of Grand Lodge for its
competency and dedication.

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNlA

De_gre.e Teams (Grand Master Channon's Recommendation No. 9,
1989 Proceedings, pages 155, 156)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
Advertising (Grand Master Channon's Recommendation No.13, 1989
Proceeding.s, pages 161, 162, 163)

My Brethren:

I am pleased to prese.nl this, my tenth annual report, to the members of the
Grand Lodge. This report is rendered in accordance with Section 1108 of the
California Masonic Code and covers the. fiscal period ending June 30, 1990.

The office of Grand Secretary carries with it the related duties of Secretary
to the Boards of Trustees of the Masonic Homes, the Memorial Temple, the
Masonic Foundation, and to the Retirement Plan Committee, the Investment
Committee and the Executive Committee of the Grand Lodge. Minutes of the
various meetings of the Boards and Committees held during the year are all on
file in the Grand Lodge office.

All monies which have been received in the Grand Lodge office have been
made available to the Grand Treasurer for appropriate credit to the various
entities of the Grand Lodge and are reflected in the report of the Grand
Treasurer.
An operating budget for the Grand Lodge office for the 1990 - 1991 fiscal
year was developed during July of this year and submitted to the Grand
Treasurer and the Finance Committee Chairman for their respective review and
approval. The Finance Committee met with the Executive Committee in August
and the balance of the Grand Lodge budget was determined. The total budget
along with the resultant per capita assessment has been distributed to all
Lod~es, as is ow custom, and will be verbally presented to you dwing the course
of this Annual Communication by the Finance Committee.

It should be boume in mind that if the amendment concerns an increase in
the Lodge dues and the Lodge has a life membership plan in effect, the fee for
purchase of that life membership must be amended to maintain the same ratio
as prescribed in California Masonic Code Section 2804. The life membership
amendment, if required, may be presented as a companion to the dues amendment, thus taking care of both amendments at the same time.
Loose Leaf Grand Lodge Roster

As you registered for this Annual Communication, each Grand Lodge
Officer, Past Grand Master, Committeeman, Inspector and Lodge Secretary
received a new 6x9 binder, imprinted with the Grand Lodge seal, together with
a set of pages which will provide you with all the information formerly published
in what we have previously printed as the Preliminary Grand Lodge Roster.
Over the years of publishing both a Preliminary and a final Roster, we have
watched the cost of editing, typesetting and printing skyrocket without being
able to do very much about it. With the purchase and implementation of the
Desktop Publishing system in 1988 and with the addition of a new upgraded
copier for the Supply Department, it is finally possible to publish this information in a more efficient and cost effective way.

Internal Revenue Guidelines
To. have a "q_ua~ed fund-raising campai~", an or~anization seeking taxdeductible contnbutwns on behalf of a qualified chanty must tell potential
donors how much of their contribution is deductible. If it w'ould be too cumbersome to tell donors the fair mark.et value of each premi~ offered, a charity can
~k t1!~ lntern!l1 Revenue Sernce to rule on alternative procedure. "Token
items mclude 1tei;ns such as bookmarks, calendars, key chains, mugs, T-shirts
and posters. Th~ item must be a "low-cost article" costing the organization no
more than $5.45 m 1990. As an example, a Lodge has a barbeque as a fund-raising event for the California Masonic Foundation. The actual cost of the barbeque ~ ~5.00 per plate. The charge for the barbeque is $10.00 per plate. Tickets,
publicity, etc. must show that only $5.00 can be classified as a tax-deductible
item.
It is most important to determine the fair market value of the benefits
offered for contributions in advance of a solicitation and to state in the solicitation and on tickets, receipts, or other documents issued in connection with a
contribution, how much is deductible under Section 170 of the Internal Revenue
C:od~ and how much is not. Keep a file copy of all printed materials you
distnbute. If unable to make an exact determination of the fair market value of
the benefits, Revenue Ruling 67-246 indicates that you should use a reasonable
estimate of the fair market value.

The pages you have received have been done completely in-house and will
have saved this Grand Lodge many thousands of dollars when the balance of
the final Roster is completed. The savings, however, is not just in the printing
of these two books, but in the mailing costs as well. We are now able to
hand-deliver the Preliminary Roster to those delegates who attend the Annual
Communication, thus saving the cost of one entire mailing. This mailing
amounts to a considerable sum of money.

If an organization is providing only unsubstantial benefits in return for a
contribution, fund-raising material should include a statement to the effect that
"Unc;ler l~ternal Reven~e Service guidelines the estimated value of the benefit
received is not subGtanual; therefore, the full amount of your contribution is a
deductible contribution.".

Shortly after January 1, 1991, the same individuals will receive the pages
which will constitute the balance of the final Roster. Pages to handle corrections
or additions will be furnished at this time also, so that you may insert them as
replacement for the pages you have received at this Communication.

For those individuals making donations of articles with a value of more than
~500.00, and for which_ th~Y. will take a charitable deduction on their personal
~com~ tax return, the 10diV1dual must file a Form 8283 signed by the organization with the tax return.

In the future, all corrections will be furnished on a quarterly basis to those
individuals holding a current Roster through the use of replacement pages.

Should you require a replacement binder Roster, the same charge will apply.

office continues to provide the membership of this Grand Jurisdiction with the
best quality and service for the dollars spent, which is the basic premise of this
office.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Conclusion
In bringing my tenth annual report to a conclusion, I must again express my
great appreciation to all those with whom the office maintains contact on an
on-going basis. We enjoy a fine working relationship with these dedicated
Masons.
I must also express appreciation to the office staff for the effort it puts forth

in accomplishing its respective functions. Increasing demands are continually
made on the Grand Lodge office and without the staff's willingness to meet
these demands, it would require additional personnel at an increased cost.
My thanks are extended to the Elective Line Officers, especially to Grand
Master Pavlovich for the warm and friendly relationship which is my extreme
pleasure to enjoy, and lastly to the members of the Grand Lodge for the privilege
of being able to serve.

Respectfully submitted,

~~
Grand Secretary

Trial Record No. 2314

Therefore kindly reserve the enclosed Amended Charges and spell

In Trial Record No. 2314, a member of Crossroads Lodge No. 696 was
charged with possession with intent to distribute cocaine and carrying and use
of a firearm during a drug trafficking crime.

Despite this, no amendment of charges was made.

The accused did not respond to the aforesaid charges. The Trial Master
found him guilty of both charges and set the penalty at suspension.

A similar recitation could be made (and has been made) about other trial
records submitted to the Grand Lodge.
Due process inour ~rial proceedin~ req~es that the member accused be
given nottce of the specific charges against him.
He can then admit or deny the charges. (J:le can also fail to re.spond to the
charges, but bis failure to respond is not sufficient proof for the Tnal Master to
fmd the charges true.)
To a layman all this may seem over-technical. It could be said "He had notice
in Court of the charges. He was found guilty. What do we have lo do?"
But acquittal in the public Court does not prevent a Masonic Tri~ (S.ection
3370), and a conviction in a Court ~oes .not prevent a second tnaf m ~ur
"Masonic Court", where the member lS entttlcd to the same safeguards as ma
public Courtroom.
This is our law and it has been stated many times. But it is vi<?lated often.
And record after record indicates the confusion of Lodges, despite words of
instruction where were thought lo be clear.
When so many make the same mistakes the language of the Code and
instructions must be inadequate.
Therefore, without abandoning thelrinciples and rules governing us, for
good reasons which appear in the recor we affirm.
But we commit ourselves to aiding Lodges avoid this problem in drafting
charges. We expect to prepare a booklet which can be mailed by the Grand
Secretary with the necessary forms.
This affirmance is not intended as a precedent, but as an exception.
Your Commitee therefore submits the following Resolution:

The Trial Master incorrectly states in the record that it was his duty to
declare the accused guilty of the charges because the accused did not respond.
U oder Masonic Law, the Trial Master must make an investigation of the charges
regardless of whether the accused does or does not respond. The Trial Master
did make an investigation and the evidence produced at Trial was sufficient for
a finding of guilty on both counts so the error was harmless herein.
We therefore submit the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that in Trial Record No. 2314, the finding of guilty of
both specifications be affirmed and the Penalty be Expulsion.
Report ADOPTED.

Trial Record No. 2316
In Trial Record No. 2316, a member ofBlacmer Lodge No. 442 was charged
with unmasonic conduct upon four specificatioflS. The member entered a plea
of Not Guilty. A Masonic Trial was held by Commission.
The Lodge elected eight (8) Commissioners. However, the trial record
indicates that only five (5) Commissioners participated in the trial, deliberations
and verdict. The Commissioners found the member ~ty of two specifications
of unmasonic conduct and set the penalty at Expulsion.
California Masonic Code Section 3346 provides that the Lodge shall, by a
vote of the Lodge, determine the number of Commissioners (not less than seven
nor more than nine). Here that procedure was followe.d with the Lodge voting
for eight (8) Commissioners.
At the Trial of the matter, only five (5) Commissioners were present.
California Masonic Code Section 3362 provides in part "...Vacancies on the
Commission, because of objection or otherwise, shall be filled by the remaining
Commissioners, subject to the approval of the Trial Master, from qualified

112

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

members of the Lodge; provided that if the majority of the Commissioners are
unable to act the Trial Master shall refer the matter to the Lodge for the election
of new Commissioners to f tll the vacancies." This procedure was not followed.
The Commissioners present at the trial should have filled the three (3)
vacancies, subject to approval of the Trial Master, from qualified members of
the Lodge so that the Masonic Trial could have proceeded without delay.
Based upon the foregoing, your Committee on Trial Review believes that
the accused member was deprived of a fair hearing in violation of California
Masonic Code Section 3362 because only five (5) Commissioners participated
in the Trial.
We therefore submit the following Resolution:
RESOLVED that the findings of Guility of unmasonic conduct and
the Penalty of Expulsion be reversed and a new Trial be conducted in
accordance with ihe California Masonic Code.
Report ADOPTED.
Trial Record No. 2252

In Trial Record No. 2252, a former member of La Mesa Lodge No. 407 was
charged with unmasonic conduct in that he did misappropriate property of
others by fraudently changing numerous return merchandise memos in violation
of California Penal Code Sections 484 and 488.
After Trial by Commission, he was found Guilty of unmasonic conduct, the
penalty was set at reprimand and Grand Lodge raised the penalty to Suspension
in October, 1987 .in recognition of the severity of the crime.
He ~as now applied for Restoration and the Lodge unanimously voted for
RestoratJon.
Your Committee on Trial Review believes that the numerous acts of the
former member arc of sufficient severity that Restoration should be denied The
conduct of the former member consisted of numerous thefts over a substantial
period of time against his employer resulting in substantial loss of money to his
employer.

This continuous conduct violated the basic tenets of trust which is expected
of every Mason.
Too little time has passed considering his former leadership in Youth

Gro~ps and the severity of the ~asonic conduct. for your Committee on Trial

Review to recommend Restoration. Moreover, his request for Restoration to
Grand Lodge does not indicate sufficient remorse on his part.

We therefore submit the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the Petition for Restoration in Trial Record No. 2252
be denied.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

MASONIC HOMES REPORT
Brethren of Grand Lodge:
When we speak of the strength and beauty of Masonry in California, there
is no better example than our Masonic Homes. From the founding of the Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons in this Jurisdiction in 1850, the Brethren
have been ever mindful of the need to provide assistance for a distressed worthy
Brother, his wife, widow or children. Our beautiful Homes in Union City and
Covina, stand as living monuments to the generous support of thousands of
Brethren through these many years.
With the completion of the latest building projects at both Union City and
Covina this past year, the new facilities are now in use. We have eve.ry reason to
be proud of the care we are able to provide for our residents, both adults and
children.
At Union City the project consisted of the Lorber Building for Skilled
Nursing care, the Siminoff Center where the new Lodge rooms are located, a
new Administrator's residence and a second access road for safety purposes.
The total completed cost was just under $16 million dollars.
At Covina, the project consisted of fifty-six apartments for adults and an
Administrative Building with a total cost ofSS,458,000. These projects were paid
for from the general funds of the Masonic Homes. Adults are now being
admitted into the Home at Covina. This is in addition to the operation of the
Children's Home, which is separate from the adults. The adult's facility in
Covina is for ambulatory residents only. At the present time, we do not have
facilities there for Personal or Skilled Nursing care. The capacity of our Homes
at present is a maximum of eighty children and approximately one hundred
adults at Covina, and four hundred adults at Union City. Due to adult applicants
coming to the Homes at a more advanced age, the ne.ed for both Personal and
Skilled Nursing care continues to increase.
A written "Masonic Homes Trustees Report", covering your Masonic
Homes operations, is included in your Grand Lodge packet of reports and we
urge you to review the details that are presented.
In the Report you will find instructions relative to the procedure for your
members to use to make application for admission to the Homes or for Nonresident Assistance.
During the week following the Annual Communication last year, there was
a severe earthquake here in the Bay Area with extensive damage and loss of life
in San Francisco, Oakland and the Santa Cruz areas. There was almost no
damage to this building or the buildings at Union City.
Considerable research and study by seismologists and U .S. Geological
Survey people is continuing in this area on potential future earthquakes. This

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

129

study includes the Hayward Fault that runs through the Union City Homes
property. The State of California has man~ated ~at ~iti~s take into consideration and implement any needed changes 10 their building eo<;fe~ that may_be
needed for additional safety. This may apply to some of our buildings at Uruon
City.
Since the earthquake last year, we have carefully reviewed our preparedness plans for future survivaJ in case of emergency. It IS essentiaJ t_o be prepared
to have food, water, utilities, bedding, blankets, first aid materials and much
more for up to seven days following an emergency.
We are carefully studying all available data on this entire subject in order
that we may take whatever action is needed for the safety of our residents and
employees.
A word about fmances. Total costs of our Homes operations for the fiscal
year ending June 30, 1990 were $17,25~,000. .Ten years ago the cost t~taled
$5,250,000. The cost has more than tripled 10 ten years. Due lo contmucd
contributions for mor~ than e~ty years ~o our Homes Endowment Fund, along
with many generous gifts provided by Wills and Bequests, our.annu~ ~ecessary
income is available without any assessment to the membership. This IS a great
tribute to the charity of Masons in this Jurisdiction. Figures from other Jurisdictions indicate that it is quite common to have an assessment of as much a $10
or more added to the per capita to support their charitable needs.
A word about Nonresident Assistance. Not all distressed Brethren, their
widows or families, need to solve their problem by moving to the Masonic
Homes. In some cases, additional funds to supplement meager pensions or
income, will assist in their remaining where they are. In such cases they
retain their independence and the cost is less for the Homes to provide
assistance.
