There are other ways to lend a helping hand. There are times that Senior
Citizens need information relative to obtaining services available through l'?C31
agencies such as Legal Assistance to Elders, Adult Day Care, transportauon,
in-home health care, homemakers services and Meals-on-Wheels.
Masonic Lodges can provide useful information to their members and
widows by use of the new "Resources Guide for Seniors". This information has
been compiled by the Grand Lodge Masonic Homes Director of Outreach
Services Kira Reginato. There are thirty-eight subjects listed in the easy to use
Table of Contents. These range from general information to making applications for admission to th.e Masonic Homes or for Nonresident Assistance
programs. These "Resources Guides" will soon be available to each Lodge
through the Homes Endowment representatives.
It is hoped that each Lodge will become a Senior Citizen Information
Center for its members.

corporation organized under the laws of the State of California, respectfully
presents its ninety-eighth annual report of the Masonic Homes of California for
the fiscal year July 1, 1989 through June 30, 1990.

for the purpose of organization. The election of Ronald A . Sherod (699),

became members of the Board ex-officio. ln addition to the Grand Lodge

Brother John A. Rose (324) has completed his ninth year as the Administrator at the Home in Covina.
Our Homes Representatives, along with Lodge Committees, interview our
applicants for admission to the Homes and those for Non-Resident Assistance.
Meetings
Meetings of the Trustees are usually held on the first Wednesday of the
month, alternating between the Union City and Covina Homes.
The meetings are frequently attended by the Chairman of the Endowment
Board, as well as some of the Endowment Board members.
Many Committee meetings are held on the Tuesday evening preceeding the
regular meeting. Most of the Committee reports are prepared m advance for
distribution at or prior to the regular meeting.
Applications for Assistance
Historically, the function of the Masonic Homes, is to assist the constil uent

approv~ by the Gr~d Lodge, are set forth in the Appendix to the California

The procedrual steps are: (1) The Lodge Secretary writes or phones to the

~or CO!llpletion; (3) the Worshipful Master appaints a three man Committee to

133

upon each applicant on the Agenda; (11) if the Trustees approve the application, the G.rand S~cretary notifies t~e Lodge and arr~gements are mad.e
administratively to unplement the relief approved; (12) if the Trustees fmd 1t

is necessary that all assets surrendered to the Homes have an appraised value
established and that they be held for a minimum of ninety days. If the resident
changes bis or her mind and wishes to leave the Home, their assets are returned
to them.
These procedrual steps have been outlined to emphasize the importance
of orderly and prompt handling of all applications, the essential role of the
constituent Lodge and the fact that applications must be processed by and
through the Lodge before they can come before the Board of Trustees. Whenever the officers of a Lodge have any question regarding procedures, we
earnestly urge that they contact the Grand Secretary by letter or telephone. In
his capacity as Secretary of the Masonic Homes, he will see that they have a
prompt answer to their problem.
Non-Resident Assistance Relief
The record sh6ws that as early as 1935 the Board of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes were confronted with r equests for assistance for those who would not
otherwise qualify for admission to the Homes. ln their report to the Grand
Lodge under the heading of Outside Relief, the Board recommended, and
Grand Lodge approved, the following statement:
"Instead of admission to the Home, outside assistance may be
granted in cases where, in the opinion of the Trustees, applicants can be better or more economically cared for outside
the Homes."
Then they proceeded to give the circumstances under which outside assistance may be granted. Then follows the three conditions which are now stated
in the Supplement of the California Masonic Code on pages 62 and 63. They
further indicated, "It is not the policy to give outside relief for temporary needs,
such relief being the duty of the Lodge direct.".

At approximately 5:00 p.m. on Tuesday, October 17, 1989, a severe
earthquake struck the Bay Area from San Francisco, east across the bay to
Oakland and south to the Santa Cruz-Watsonville area. Damage was extensive
including loss of life and many injuries.

eoordination with the Masonic Homes Repre5entative, the Administrators of
Union City and Covina, and the balance of the Committee in all matters
concerning Admissions. In addition, the Committee continues to review and
update all appli.cation forms and admission policies to insure a compliance with
current reguJat1ons.

Only minor dama~e occurred at the Home in Union City and the Masonic
Memorial Temple building in San Franciso. Due to the Grand Lodge office
being closed for seve.r al days, the November Board of Trustees meeting was
postponed one week because of the delay in paperwork in preparation for the
meeting.

We acknowledge with genuine thanks the outstanding cooperation of
Committee members Warren Blomseth, Warren Buschmann, Stephen Doan,
Verl Lobb, Gene Perkins, Gerald Sharer and the assistance by Administrators
Paul Boyar and John Rose.

The subsequent actions of the State of California caused a complete
re-examination of the structural integrity of our buildings and site facilities at
Union City.

by Gerald A. Sharer, Chairman Real Estate Committee

We employed a structural engineering firm to ascertain if we were in
compliance with the earthquake code adopted by Union City as mandated by
the State of California. They h ave advised us that the Code as adopted does not
apply to our main buildings but precedence requires modification to some of
the older structures.

The function of the Committee is to dis~se of Real Estate made available
to the Masonic Homes by residents' gifts, wills and other bequests.

The old boiler house which is currently being used as a storage area is not
in compliance and will be demolished.
All of the site utilities are being studied from the standpoint of earthquake
preparedness. Since all of our services cross the Hayward Fa wt wc are proVJding
on-site alternatives for emergency back up. In this regard we have learned that
the main water supply tank has several serious cracks and a new structural lining
is being designed.
A remodeling of portions of the kitche n of the Sedam Central Services
building will be undertaken in the coming fiscal year. This area serves the entire
facility and is the refore subject to heavy usage which has necessitated upgrading. The estimated cost will be $350,000.00.
We have had a consulting engineer make a survey and report on the
Emergency Preparedness plans for "7 days sufficiency" inside and outside of the
buildings in case of a severe earthquake on the Hayward Fault.

Scholarships
by Jack R. Vickers, Chairman Scholarship Committee

For a great number of years the Masons of California have supported a
Scholarship Program for our children at the Covina Home. This has been made
possible througli the Wills and Bequests by our concerned Brethren. Over the
years these Trusts have been prudently invested by the Board of Trustees so
that Scholarship Grants and Loans may be made from the earnings of these
trusts without a.ny depletion of the principal. Over the past twelve (12) years a
total of $324,927 bas been awarded to thirty-six of our deserving young people
to assist in their formal education.
Scholarship Grants and Loans are awarded on specific need and are based
upon the specific academic level; Junior College, Vocational Schoo~ Colle~e,
Universicy, and Post Graduate School. The value of Scholarship Grants vanes
with the academic level being attempted. For example, a maximum Grant of
$4,000 is available to those applicants who are undertaking Junior College or
Vocational School level studies. To those at the State College or equivalent
leve~ a maximum Grant of $4,600 is available. Those studying at the University
level have a maximum Grant available of$5,800, and those who are undertaking
Post Graduate Studies may receive a maximum Grant of $6,900. In few cases
where costs exceed the maximum allowable Grant, loans are made available.
These loans are repayable to the Board after the student has graduated and is
established in the community.
Applicants are required to make formal application on a yearly basis to the
Board of Trustees through the Scholarship Committee. The Committee

REPORT OF THE ADMINI STRATO R
MASON IC HOME, UNION Cl1Y
1989 -1990
At the dawn of a new decade I would look forward to the 1990's and beyond,
a period that holds bright promise for the Masonic Home at Union City.
The challenge of the 90's for ow Home will be to continue to provide the
highest quality of resident services in a social and economic unstable futwe. In
order to ~de us in the accomplishment of this goal we have made the following
assumpt10ns:
1. Resident s will primarily be persons born from 1900 to 1920. Ow
cwrent average age is 86. The 85 + poP.ulation is growing faster than
any other group and our average age will increase over time.
2. Longevity has improved and expectati ons relative to quality of life
and health care will be dramatic.
3. Cost of care will continue to grow at a rate exceeding 10% annually.
W~can control t_hese costs wi~hout reducing services. It will be our goal
to increase and unprove seMces.
4. Shortage s of skilled labor will continue. Recruitm ent, training,
employee retention and morale will take an increasin g share of our time
and firiancial resources.
5. The residents of the 90's will be in need of more expensive Personal
and Skilled Nursing services. Medical needs and costs will soar as ow
average age increases .
In anticipati on of these new directions, the Home has embarke d this past
year on a program which will lay the groundw ork for the future.
First, we have redefined the organizations' functions, goals and objectives.
Various internal managem ent procedur es and lines of authority, including
budget responsibilities, were reorganiz ed to produce maximum efficiency,
effectiveness and accountability. We belive that in order to be ready to service
the next generatio n of Masons, their wives and widows, we need to establish
progressi ve management concepts today.
Our next step was to realize that the delivery of physician services is the key
element of tomorrow . After an excellent 40 year relationsh ip with Palo Alto
Medical Foundati on, the Foundati on notified us of their intent to withdraw
Primary Care Services at the Home. Specialty care would continue at Palo Alto.
At this point we decided to abandon the fee for service concept of care and
embark upon a system of full time salaried physician services. This theory
became a reality with the hiring of Dr. Dennis Stone in October 1989. Joining
Dr. Stone, on salary, was another part-time Physician and a Nurse Practition er.
This group helped expand our physician coverage 200%.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFO RNIA

This change, like many of the others that followed, was not easily assimilated into our exis~g system. As we enter our second year:, these .seMces.b ave

bcCODlC int.tegrated into our structure and we are producm g a high

quality of
·dent Health Care. The delivery of medical services will be enhanced during
next year by the .bringing of s~alty physician services to the Home instead
of [)oetors' offices in the commuruty.

Another concern was employee morale. Before any new benefit program
could be instituted, some employee s petitione d for union represent ation. We
put on a major team effort to defeat this attempt, and were successfu l We were
then able to implemen t a ~jor employee salary and benefit program which has
translated into better and higher morale.

projects that needed our immedia te attention. We purchase d:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Our main dining room will receive all new tables, chairs, carpets, window
and floor coverings.
Plans also call for the expenditure of over $500,000 on equipment replacement and upgrades throughout the Home.
Enhancing the future needs of the Home, was the opening of the magnificent Lorber Skilled Nwsing Facility in January 1990. This regal testimony
to the Craft's never-end.in~ goal of giving the very best care, can be seen on a
daily basis within this facility. The luxurious rooms for patient and dining and
the state-of-the-art nursing stations and common areas, makes caring for our
Brothers, their wives and widows easier.
Identifying the need for expanded resident spiritual, social and activity
services, prompted us to double the size of those three departments. Two new
Master's Degree Social Workers were hired, along with three additional Activity Leaders and a second Chaplain.
Rehabilitation services, the cornerstone of progressive Skilled Nursing
Care, received a major boost when Progressions Health Care joined our team,
supplying the Home with two full-time Physical Therapists, a full-time Occupational Therapist and a Speech Therapist. Our Home's Rehab Department can
be considered one of the leaders in the field.
The past year saw a major shift in our health care philosophy. We now allow
residents .in Residential and Personal Care to remain in their apartments as long
as posstble before being transferred to the Skilled Nur~ Facility. "Aging in
place" supported by a system of Home-based care supplied by a locaf home
health agency and our Nurse Practitioner, keeps residents at home for as long
as possible. This program, monitored by our Nurse and Doctor, brings the
highest level of care right into the residents' living rooms, preventing in many
cases, the needless uprooting of individuals and placement into the Skilled
Nursing Facility.
As you can see, it has been an eventful year with many new and exciting
programs and changes.

Your Home received a new State designation in January 1990, as a "Life
Care Community". We have evolved as a community that offers a full range of
housing. residential and health care services. Our goal is to serve our residents
over time as their physical and mental needs change. This continuum of care
consists of housing where residents live indepenaently and receive certain
residential services, such as meals, activities, housekeeping and maintenance.
Support Services for disabled residents who require assistance with activities of
daily living and health care services for those who become temporarily ill or who
require long term care are also provided.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

145

Residents who age in place present challenges to management. We strive
to enrich services to frail residents who are already dealing with the normal
losses that come with age and physical disability. We try lo meet the sometimes
conflicting needs of long-time guests with those of incoming and future residents. With the counsel of the Board of Trustees, I look forward to the next year
and years to come. We will contine to provide the very best care to these
wonderful residents the Craft bas placed m our care.
Respectfully submitted,
Paul M. Boyar,Administraror

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Why So Few Children at Covina?
The number of children being served at Covina diminished for a number
of internal and external reasons.

The Evolution at Covina

1. Common diseases which formerly left many children orphaned have
been eliminated.

This past year has been one ~f rapid, albeit planned change. Your Masonic
Home at Covina has completed its planned expansion. Our lofty goal to fill a
greater need has come to fruitation.

2. We are not presently confronted with a.severe eronomic condition
such as the haishness of the great depreSSion.

. Originally in 1899, the Masonic Home served both the elderly and the
~hildren at ~e?Oto, now Union City. The children moved to a separate Home
m San Gabnel 10 1906 and later to Covina. Since 1917 and until January 8 1990
'
'
the Masonic Home at Covina was solely a children's Home.
In our early history, the number of children placed in the Masonic Home

~ough distressed Masons and .their wives ~d -.yidows were as many as 180. In

VJew of a reduced number of childen at Covina, its 33 acres were not efficiently
used even though the care program remained highly effective. Your Trustees
~ertly.combin~d .t~eir perception of increased need for adult program expansion with the diminished need for the property at Covina.

T~y we ~ve gone "... back to the future". The trend in the gerontology
.

program, ha~ been constructed on available property at Covina, allows not
only a mo~e effic1e.nt use but we have become a most innovative congregate living
program m Amenca.
The Covina Adult Program
Today the wisdom of the elderly, the strength and vitality of children and
the ~eaut):' of th~m both adorn the Masonic Home at Covina. The voluntary
re~tJonships which have formed between many of our children and elderly
residents has a synergistic effect and multiplies the benefits to both.

T~e Cali1:ornia Department of Social Services granted the Masonic Home
at Covma a license to operate as a Residential Facility for the Elderly. On
January8, 1990,.the adult program.at Covina commenced its operations. Twelve
am~ulato~ residents from the Union City facility, having connections with
fam~y, friends and fraternal ties in Southern California, transferred to the
Covma Home. Other approved applicants were admitted by the Board of
Trustees.
. Although we have .fifty-six modem and tastefully appointed apartments

3. We are not engaged in declared war which prompted many applications in the past.
4. The establishment of county foster home programs in this jurisdiction became another altematJve to placement, particularly for those
families distant to Covina.

5. Today, _governmental support is available to families with dependent
children (AFDC).

6. For many years the various Juvenile Courts have properly de-emphasized placement of children in group homes in favor of children
remaining in the immediate family, with relatives, through adoption or
in foster homes.
7. The population of Masons is declining and the average age is
increasing. Fewer applications are being received to assist the sons and
daughters of ~asons and their wives or widows.
8. Lack of knowledge that the Masonic Home can serve grandchildren.
nieces, nephews and other next-of-kin relations of distressed members
and their wives or widows is another contributor to the decline in the
number of children served.
There are fifty-eight (58) Masonic-related Homes in America. For reasons
generally related to governmental encroachment and reduced populations, only
nine (9) Masonic Children's Homes remain. In addition to California, these
Homes are in Georgia, Illinois, Mississipp~ Nebraska, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas and Louisiana.
In order to maintain their philanthropic service to childre~, these other
jurisdictions elected to expand their service to the non-Masorucally related
child. California, in accordance with the California Masonic Code and its
original mission. requires Masonic Relationship as one of the prerequisites for
admission into its Children's Home.

1. The average stay in foster homes is too short.
2. There are too few foster homes.
3. Frequent moves compromise consistency so essential to children.
4. Funding dollars have been abused and may not find their way into
the lives ol the children being served.

5. The children are often not fully pregared to be adults at eighteen
years of age and upon discharge from the system".
6. It is not always possible to serve brothers and sisters in the same
foster home.
7. The strong emphasis to return dependent children to the family,
although laudable, has resulted in further trauma to many children.

8. Often delinquent children are commingled with dependent children
resulting in more confusion for the victim children.
Today many child care professionals are calling to utilize, to a fuller extent,
quality group homes. Quality group homes are those which seek to meet the
needs, serve and protect those qualified for admission. Althou$h prudent and
cautious with their funding, such group homes are not solely mollvated by profit.

bears witness that-to relieve the distressed is a duty incumbent upon all men,
but particularly upon Masons. As your Administrator, I wish to thank you for
having done this so well.

PROCEEDING S OF THE

REPORT OF TRUSTEES
CALIFORNIA ~ONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE

Your Board of Trustees meets quarterly and this year we have accomplished the following:
Internal Revenue Service Audit

Your Memorial Temple was graced this year by the Internal Revenue
Service conductin~ an inspection ofour re.cords and accounting procedures for
the fiscal year ending June 30, 1987. It revealed the account~ firm of Lindquisty, Von Husen and Joyce was remiss by the inconsistent and maccurate filirig of
reports with the Internal Revenue Service Fresno Service Center which very
easily could have triggered this audit.
I am happy to report the Internal Revenue Service District Director, by his
!etter of June 14, 1990, advised the Grand Lodge of California there is no ch~e
m the exempt status of the Memorial Temple as described in Section 501(c)(3)
of the Internal Revenue Code. However, the Temple has been reclassified
i:nder S~c~on 509(a) of the Code to an organization which is a private foundallon. This is based on the assumption that current operations will remain the
same.
The Memorial Temple is a private foundation, and pays a two percent (2%)
quarterly estimated tax, due to the unrelated income generated by the garage
and the Pine Street property.
Financial Reserves

Two years ago, the Memorial Temple amended its Articles of Incorporation to establish a fmancial reserve for the repair, upkeep and maintenance of
Temple equipment. It has a present book value of $538,000. After careful
cons1derallon the Board has established a reserve of one (1) million dollars.

Memorial Temple Garage
The present lease for the operation and management of the garage expires
March 1, 1993. Prior to this date, bids from other garage operators will be
solicited, to assist the Board in making its decision for future garage management.

REPORT OF THE COMMITI'EE ON
RECOGNITIO N OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The function of this Committee is primarily d etermined by the established
standards of Masonic recognition in California which are:
1) Legitmacy of origin
2) Exclusive territorial jurisdiction ( This is clarified in Article II,
Annotations 7, 7a and 7b of the California Masonic Code)
3) Adherence to the ancient landmarks.
Investigations of all organizations reques ting recognition as regular
Masonic Grand Lodges are carried out as needed and reported to the Grand
Master as well as at the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, with
appropriate recomme.n dations, if any. In addition, information furnished by
other regular Masonic Grand Lodge bodies and the reports of the investigations
conducted by the Grand M asters of Masons in North America Commission on
Information and Recognition, are considered.
L Concernin2 the Grand Lod&e of Iran (in exile)· After communication
with the Secretary-Treas urer of the Conference of Grand Masters of Masons
in North America, and after a year-long on-going investigative process initiated
here in this Masonic jurisdiction, it is recommended that recognition of the
Grand Lodge of Iran ( m exile) be denied, and that it be considered a clandestine
organization. The attached directive "Subject A" is relevant to this matter and
reveals some serious causes for concern. It was sent by Grand Master Sam M.
Pavlovich to all Lodge Secretaries in August of this year, 1990, and is self-explanatory.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

173

z._ Austria-Hun2acy: After nearly 40 years of banishment and Masonic
darkness, Hungarian brethren were joined lD Budapest by the Grand Lodge of
Austria in consecrating the Symbolic Grand Lodge of Hungary and installing
its officers. The Grand Lod~e of Austria is recognized by all Grand Lodges of
the United States and it is sm cerely hoped that this event marks the beginning
of the rebuilding of Freemasonry in Eastern Europe. It is still true that where
there is no freedom in this world, there is no Freemasonry, and that where
freedom flourishes, so does the Craft.

J The Grand Orient of Italy: Secretary of the Commission, Robert L .

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON CODE REVISION

The total registration is made up as follows:

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
This Committee was created at the 1988 Annual Communication with the
charge "to prepare a revised Code written in clearer language to be presented
for adoption at the subsequent Annual Communication.".
At the last Annual Communication, the Committee reported its progress
to simplify the language of Code Sections, eliminate ambiguities and seek
consistency in language and format
Since the last Annual Communication, some issues, then unresolved, have
been determined. A loose-leaf Code book to contain a glossary and a more
workable index are among them.
The Committee has determined that a revised Code, containing no substantive law changes, will be the result of its work. The Committee on Jurisprudence
has been consulted to assist with interpretations and ambiguities to this end.
It is contemplated that the Committee work can be completed in time for
presentation to the Grand Lodge at the 1991 Annual Communication.

REORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE
ON FEES AND DUES STRUCTIJRE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
This Committee was established at the recommendation of Most Worshipful Stanley L. Channon, Past Grand Master, to study the Fees and Dues
structure of the constituent Lodges of this Jurisdiction and to report their
findings and to make recommendations. First, it is the opinion of the Committee
members that any change to the Fees or Dues structure of the constituent
Lodges should come from the Lodges themselves and not be dictated by action
of Grand Lodge. Each Lodge has the responsiblity to act in a manner which will
enhance their o~ ~dge, and e~ta?lishing appr~priate D~es and Fees are part
of that responsibility. Second, it IS the Committee's belief that each I..Odge
should carefully review their own Dues and Fees and update them so that they
more closely reflect the inflation rate that has taken place over the last several
years.
As I am sure you are aware, the more activities that a Lodge has, and the
more involved that its members are with these activities, the more new candidates that the Lodge will take in and the easier it will be to obtain officers.
There is a saying, "The more successful that an organization is, the more people
want to join and become a part of it". Although having money, as generated
through Dues and Fees, will not automatically give you that success, using that

183

GRAND WOGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

1Doney (or activities and communications with the members can make it pos510tc. With this thought in mind, let's look at the Fees and Dues of the constituent
Lodges.
The Committee selected four different years for the review of the Fees and

Dues; these years were 1989, 1984, 1979 and 1967. 19891 1984 and 1979 afford

the opportunity to look at three five (5) year intervals auring the most recent
ten year history. 1967 was selected because it was the first year the Consumer
Price Index (CPI) was established. The CPI for 1967 was 100 and in 1989 it was
approximately 384- almost four times (384% ) the 1967 level. The average Dues
for 540 Lodges in 1989 were $32.30, while in 1967 they were $18.34 for 711
Lodges. The avt:rase increase has only been 32% . S~arly, the Fees in 1989
were $105.96 while 10 1967 they were $93.44, an average mcrcase of about 13%.
Thus, we see that our Lodges have slowly changed their Fees and Dues structure
over the past ten years. However, they still have not kept up with inflation. If we
calculate the CPI increase over the past 22 years, we should be paying an average
of $70.39 for Dues and $358.62 for Fees just to stay even with inflation!

The chart above shows that four (4) Lodges in 1989 charge the minimum
of $12.00 allowed by the California Masonic Code. Only one of these I....odses
has any significant amount of money left over (approximately $950) after paying
their Per Capita tax; one of them only as $83 left. My Brethren, how can you run
a Lodge on only $83 per year? Yes, we have been told that some of these Lodges
have more than $1 million in the bank and if they need anything they just draw
on these funds. But, most Lodges do not have that luxury. As a matter of fact,
many ~es, when rcferri~ to one or more of the Grand Lodge Programs that
they shoufa support, complain that "we can't afford that". However, a member
of one Lodge that has the minimum dues, stated that they don't need to increase

184

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

their dues because if they need money they just assess their members or charge
more for their activities. This Lodge is now merging with another Lodge becauac
they did not have enough members willing to take their officer positions. Is thia
due to lack of money? Probably not directly; however, it would seem that if more
money had been available they might have bad more activities, invol~~.more
of their members and consequently more members might have been willing lo
take officer positions.
Unfortunately, it's a perverse aspect of human nature that unless some~
is expensive it isn't worth having and our Lodge Fees and Dues tell some~
about us. We do not value our own worth enough to charge what we should lo
be a member; this is true for both joining and continuing our membership. What
do our own members have to say about thLc;? A recent study funded by the
Scottish Rite showed that "Masons don't need to attend Lodge to achieve
satisfaction, nor is there a compelling reason to maintain membership - except
pride - and dues are so low that it doesn't make a real difference". Isn't that the
real story! Our members DON'T CARE about attending Lodge because they
don't have any reason to, and they only maintain their membership because IT
COSTS SO LIITLE to do so.
So why not raise the Lodge Dues if it would make our members feel that it
was important to belong? The familiar refrain is recited, "We would loose half
of our members" or "Our older members can't afford to have the Dues increased,
they are on a fixed income". First, the Lodge will not loose half the members.
Certainly so.me will Dimit to another "cheaper" Lodge, but experience has
shown that most will stay. Second, most members who are on fixed incomes, or
receive Social Security, receive cost of living increases every year. If you have
one of the rare members who is truly on a fixed income with no cost of living
increase, you can make special arrangemenLc; with him to remit his Dues so he
does not have to drop his membership.
Looking at Fees, a story is told about a German Lodge that wanted to limit
its membership and felt that by raising its Degree Fees the Lodge could
accomplish this purpose. The Fees were raised to $500 and now it seems that
there is a line around the building with men waiting to join the Lodge. Sounds
a little far fetched doesn't it, but it does seem to verify that if it doesn't cost a
great deal, it's not worth anything.

Some traveled great distances to attend. All had ideas with r~spect to l~e future
direction of Grand Lodge and our local Lodges. Four topics were discussed:
How can we encourage young men to become Masons? What programs should
Lodges offer? How can we interest young people in leadership roles? For what
should Masons be noted or "what do Masons do"?

How Cap We Epcouraa: Youn& Meg to Uecome Masops?
Several concerns were noted in discussion s of this question. Many young

~cause of y.'Ork and other family co~mitments. Many you_ng wives work. ~~ is
difficult to interest many young men 10 fraternal orgaruzauo ns unless families
are involved and time devoted to the or~anization's activities is used in the most
effective manner possible. The followmg suggestions were made. All Lodge
activities other than tiled meetings should include families. The programs
should be designed to interest not only Masons but their wives and children.
Activities of interest to younger people, such as sports teams, should be encouraged. We should be more active with the Masonic youth groups. Some
suggested that fewer Lodges with larger membersh ips would have tlie people
and funds to sponsor more interesting programs.
Some questioned whether our present system of candidate' s proficiencies
is the most effective use of the candidate' s time. Perhaps the same amount of
time could be devoted to an alternate proficiency system where self study
regarding the philosophy and principles of Freemason ry could be emphasii.ed
rather than memorizat ion of answers to questions. Some noted the prograim
developed by Nebraska and Tllinois in whose alternate proficiency systems the
candidate learns the signs, words and modes of recognition and studies the
philosophy of Freemason ry through personal reading and group meetings, at
the conclusion of which an open book e~tion i:; completed covering_many
of the same areas of our current profietenc1es but m greater depth and m the
candidate' s own words. It was suggested that Grand Lodge consider the appointment of a committee to study these alternate systems of candidate
proficiency with a view to adopting any of the advantages noted.
It w~ also suggested that Freemason ry is n<?t sufficien.tly_ ~~ble in the
commumty and that many young people are more 10terested 10 JOllllll8 groues
which are community oriented. This area is discussed in greater detail later m
this report. Some also expressed the belief that the perceived lack of ethnic and
religious diversity in Freemason ry inhibits some young people from joining.
Many felt that our members are unclear as to the limitations with respect
to our anti-solicit ation rules. We should do a better job of educating our C?WD
members about what may be said regarding the fraternity and how the subject

Most importantl y, many suggested that, in order to attract young people,

organize a nucleus of its younger members to plan programs to attract their
contempor aries to Lodge activities. Many Lodges have younger members who

What Pr'WJlmS Should Lo~es Offer?

wi_tho~t.mucb ch~ge or imaginatio n in their presentatio n. A variety in program-

two appr<?acbes give differing views. ~e met our goal in presenting!en Spr~g

VOTE REQUIRED FOR ADOPTION OF LEGISLATION

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Grand Master Channon's
Recommendation No. 8 has been referred, reports as follows:
Grand Master Channon recommended that to provide a more reasonable
but still cautious approach to the passage of new legislation seeking to change
our California Masonic Code, the voting requirements should be relaxed from
the present five-sixths for passage to three-quarters.
Your Committee finds that the le~lation as proposed in 1989 and as
distributed by the Grand Secretary at this Annual Communication is adequate
to carry out the intent of Grand Master Channon.
Since this Recommendation, at the last Annual Communication, received
less than the five-sixths vote required for adoption, but did receive a majority
vote, it has been carried over for reconsideration at this Annual Communication
and a two-thirds affirmative vote is now required for adoption.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In bis Recommendation No. 8, Grand Master Channon suggested that
California Masonic Law be amended so that a three-quarters majority vote by
the delegates to the Grand Lodge would effect the adoption of such legislation.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes consistently has opposed
such a change in our law and we hold lo this same principle today. Let me quote
some of the reasons slated by this Committee al our last Annual Communication.

19')

8 simple majority in favor,

it is then carried over to the following Annual
eommunicat10n, at which time only a two-thirds favorable vote is needed for
passage. Therefore, the concept that a five-sixths affirmative vote is required to
chan~e our law is fallacious. In truth, only a two-thirds affirmative vote is
reqwred to change our law.
The deliberate process now required by our law has a tendency to temper
an appeal to one's emotions. Countless times in our history an eloquent speaker,
with an emotional appeal for bis legislation, has been able to acquire the simple
majority vote which provides for carry-over to the following year. We find that
given the opportunity for deliberate reflection the delegates to the Grand Lodge
have determined that many of these matters deserved defeat and consequently
did not receive the two-thirds favorable vote the second year. I point out to you,
my Brethren, that the law can and frequently has been changed by only a
two-thirds majority vote. This carry-over Recommendation now before you
requires only a two-thirds vote for passage. However, although I have not made
an actual count, there have been numerous changes, amendments, or additions
to our law bv the full five-sixths majority vote, particularly in recent years.
Keeping the law as it now is can preserve only its benefits without adversely
affecting the constituent Lodge's ability to change the law. Your Committee
continues to believe that our present process encourages th.at mature consideration and we recommend that you vote "No" to carry-over Recommendation No.

8.

Recommendation NOT APPROVED.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Channon recommended that one or more degree teams be
permitted to perf'!rm ritual, provided that the me.m~rs of the team were hi~y
qualified and certified by the Inspector of the Distnct. Such teams to perfOrm
only at the invitation of the Master of the Lodge.
Grand Master Channon cited the large percenta~e of applicants for the
degrees of Masonry who do not advance beyond the First Degree for a variety
of reasons. One of the reasons most often cited is the poor impression gained
through the unsatisfactory presentation of the ritual.
Most Worshipful Brother Channon noted that the Ritual Committee and
the Inspectors have difficulty in achieving high quality ritual presentation by
officers of some Lodges. Reasons, or excuses, cited for this deficiency include
both the lack of time, and lack of interest in learning and becoming proficient
in the work.
One of the most important functions of a Lodge is the conferral of degrees.
From time immemorial the quality of conferral, the solemnity of the event, and
the atmosphere of spirituality have been of prime importance in. the presentation of degrees. The degrees conferred under such circumstances assure that
the candidate retains an impression of decorum and dignity.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes is in agreement with
Grand Master Channon that qualified and proficient degree teams can add to
the solemnity and impressiveness of our degrees. We also believ.e that the Lodge
attendance 101proves with the quality of the performance dunng the degrees;
that degree team members tend to be better cast to their particular parts than
Lodge Officers who are constantly changing stations; that the opportunity to be
part of a team, without becoming an officer, encourages newer members to
become involved; that team members, by their very involvement, indicate their
interest in ritual and performance. Team membership involves more Lod,ge
members and encourages more visita~ons .. We believe that the s~~lic
authorization of degree teams by resolution will encourage greater partICtpation. The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.

when he states, "The manner in which the ritual of the three degrees is presented
to the candidate is extremely important". He also correctly points out that
degree teams are already permitted within the Jurisdiction, and that many
already exist.
This Recommendation will not improve the quality of our ritual. lt allows
only what is already allowed, and, therefore, is unnecessary. It also adds a
certification requirement which could be difficult to administer.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponent of this Resolution seems to base bis desire for change solely
on the proposition that Grand Lodge does something that Constituent Lodges
are not allowed to do.
Grand Lodge, after many of its activities during the year, is often closed by
declaration by the Grand Master.
There is no regular "short form" ritual for the closing of Grand Lodge. It is
done in each instance by executive prerogative of the Grand Master.
The Grand Lodge Officers assemble from all points of California for each
Grand Lodge event, some travelling a considerable distance which requires
adhering to travel schedules not or their own making. A missed plane, for
instance, could mean a U to 24 hour delay and added expense and inconvenience to those involved. Travel by automobile, especially during inclement
weather in mountainous terrain can prove to be extra-hazardous during hours
of darkness.
Each Grand Master generally considers the well-being of his officer corps
and allows them to disperse to their homes as soon as practical following the
open ceremony.

work and costs to the Lodges. Because the contributions are received in small

Since this Resolution , at the last Annual Communic ation, received less than
the five-sixths vote required for adoption, but did receive a majority vote, it has
been carried over for reconsider allon at this Annual Communic ation and a
two-thirds affirmative vote is now required for adoption.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
There are thousands of sojourners residing within the territorial jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge. To visit one of our Lodges, a sojourner is subject to
the same requireme nts as any other visitor: demonstra te that be is in good
standing in his home Lodge, and prove that he is a Master Mason, either by
private examinatio n or avouchmen t. Thus, any Master Mason may enjoy the
fellowship of our Lodges without submitting to an Investigating Committee .
However, if such a sojourner wishes to become a member of one of our
Lodges by affiliation, he must be examined by an Investigating Committee , just
as any other prospectiv e member of the Lodge. As we noted last year, the formal
investigation looks into the applicant's physical and financial health, to determine whether he is likely to become a charge of the Lodge, or whether he is
affiliating for future admission to the Masonic Home. The investigation also
confirms that the applicant's personal conduct has continued to be above
reproach since be first joined the Craft. In short, it is designed to insure that all
new members will be an asset to the Lodge they join.
We believe that the advantages in such an investigation easily outweigh the
inconvenie nce and time involved, particularl y when the applicant is a sojourner
from another state or country. Accordingly, the Policy and General Purposes
Committee opposed this Resolution last year. Your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes again recommen ds a "No" vote.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED .

DISPLAYING APRON DURING ITS EXPLANATION
AND PRESENTATION TO A CANDIDATE

This Resolution seeks to amend the Ritual and a five-sixths affirmative vote
is required for adoption.

(90-2)

The prop_onent of this Resolution seeks to require the Master to hold the
apron up to display to the candidate during its presentation to him.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. & A.M. of California:
~REAS, it is customary to bold an object up for all to see when speaking
about It; and

~REAS, the Master holds up the Wor~ Tools to the view of the
Candidate so that he may clearly see the object that IS being spoken about; and

WHEREAS, ~uring ~e Ceremony of Installation the Master of Ceremonies
~olds up each ob1ect to View for all to see when the Installing Master mentions

it; and

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution 90-2 requires the Lodge Master to hold up the apron to display
it to the candidate during presentation to him.
The author of this Resolution feels that in giving the apron to the candidate
in the first degree prior to explaining its significance in some way detracts from
the importance of the apron.
Your Committee fails to see how having the candidate himself hold the
apron while having its s~ficance explained diminishes in any way the importance of the apron, or mmimires the emp~is of the Master' s comme~ts. ~he
apron is placed in th~ can~date's hands with the front of the apron facmg him,
and he himself holds it while the Master speaks. If anything, this serves to focus

224

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

the candidate's attention more closely on the subject of the Master's explanatory
remarks.
It is true that this is not done in the case of the trowel, but bear in mind that
when presenting the apron the Master steps down to the floor and confronts
the candidate face to face. In both cases the presentation is made at the same
time the words are stated in the recitation of the ritual.

In comparing the presentation of the apron with the working tools or the
trowel, there is another difference. The apron is the one thing that is presented
to the candidate which becomes his forever. It seems only right that he should
hold it.
Ritual changes may be made only as permitted in Section 2690. We do not
feel that such is the case in this Resolution.
We recommend a "No" vote.
The Committee on Ritual:

Throughout the presentation of our ritual, we always try to make the words
and actions complement each other. We do this for two reasons. Fust, it makes
the ritual clearer for the candidate. Secondly, it makes it more logical and easier
for those performing the ritual.
The proponent correctly states that everything to be explained is displayed
during its explanation. Of all the listed examples, though, the only objects which
are ever physically given to the candidate are the trowel and the apron, and they
are handed to him when the words of the ritual dictate their presentation. A
better example, perbaps1•is the point at which the Master "presents" his right
hand to the candidate following the obligation, joining words and action.
Your Committee on Ritual feels that the present (no pun intended) time
at which the apron is banded to the candidate is appropriate and consistent with
the standard set in the rest of the ritual. We recommend a "No" vote.

RECOGNITION OF PRINCE HALL LODGES
(90-7)

The proponent of this Resolution seeks to have the Grand Lodge of
California r~, as re~ Masonic Lodges under its jurisdiction, all
Prince Hall Lodges located 10 California.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M . &A.M. of California:

WHEREAS, Worshipful Prince Hall was a regular Mason, and a member
of African Lodge No. 459, Boston, Massachusetts; and
WHEREAS, Worshipful Prince Hall did, in 1784, seek a warrant for his own
Lodge, and, in 1787, received said warrant from the Grand Lodge of England;
and
WHEREAS, Worshipful Prince Hall regularly presided over his Lodge as
its Master for 31 years; and
WHEREAS, his Lodge did regularly send "returns and charitable contribution.ct to the Grand Lodge of England; and

WHEREAS, his Lodge, unbeknownst to Worshipful Prince Hall and the
members of his Lodge, was removed from the Grand Lodge of England in 1813
for the reason of nonpayment of dues even though records show such payments
were regularly forwarded to the Grand Lodge, and such removal was not
discovered by Hall Lodge members until 1834; and
WHEREAS, men of varying degrees of Black African ancestry have histori-

~ly been systematically excluded from participation in regular Masonic

Lodges in the United States, requiring them to seek Masonic fellowship in the
Prince Hall Lodges; and

WHEREAS, men of varying degrees ofBlack African ancestry are still beins
denied applications for membership in resuJar Masonic Lodges, even though
Califonua Section 2403 specifically prohibits such practice; and
WHEREAS, the situation of two distinct bodies of Freemasonry existing
side by side, separated solely by the ancestry of its members, and the resulting

The Committee on Jurisprudence:

The proponent of this Resolution seeks to a.mend Article II, Section 8 of
the Califorrua Masonic Code by changing the address to be given to Grand
Lodge Members and Grand Lodge Officers and adding Inspectors as Grand
Lodge Officers.
The legislation before you erroneously calls for the deletion of Annotation

U08g. As that is unnecessary, the deletion of that Annotation is removed as a
part of that legislation.

With that exception, your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand Secretary to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry
out the intent of the proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend the Constitution and Ordinances and a
five-sixths affumative vote is required for adoption.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution 90-8 proposes to change the titles given to Grand Lodge Officers and add Inspectors as Grand Lodge Officers.
This Resolution proposes to give life-Ion~ rerosmtion to all who serve
Grand Lodge in either elective or appointive positions, mcluding the Inspectors,
by conveying upon them the titles of Most Worshi{>ful, ~t Worshipful Rijdit
Reverend, or Very Worshipful depending on their office. Such titles "shall'be
cooferred for life and shall be retroactive". It would also make Inspectors G rand
Lodge Officers with the title of Very Worshipful.
Your Committee feels that life-long titles have historically been reserved
for those who held their office by virtue of election by Brethren of Grand Lodge.
To convey these honorary titles on literally hundreds of Brethren, some of whom
served as an appointive officer for only one year, perhaps decades ago, would
demean these lltles.
There are a number of unanswered questions regarding the possible import
of this Resolution. Would Inspectors, who would be now defined as Grand
Lodge Officers, join in the procession that opens each session of Grand Lodge?
Would Inspectors' attendance at Grand Lodge be mandatory? Would
Inspectors' reimbursement at Grand Lodge be on the same basis as other Grand
Lodge Officers? Would Grand Lodge be mandated to provide Inspectors with
jewels of their office as provided in Article II, Section 9 of our Constitution?
However, of greatest concern to your Committee would be the provisions
of Section 252 of our Constitution, "Each elective and appointive officer of the
Grand Lodge, except the Grand Tiler, each Past Grand Officer of the Grand
Lodge, and Master, Senior Warden, Junior Warden, and collectively the Past
Masters of a given Lodge, shall be given one vote." This Resolution defines a
Past Grand Lodge Officer as "one who has been regularly elected or appointed
and installed." Therefore, all appointive Grand Lodge Officers, which under

242

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

this Resolution would now also include all of the Inspectors,, would be entitled
to an individual vole, not only while serving in office, but tor life! This could
result in a fundamental shift in the distribution of decision making power in
Grand Lodge which could be detrimental to the interests of Constituent Lodges.
It would create a large blot of voters which would not represent any Lodge, but
would be entitled to one full vote each only by virtue of having once been a
Grand Lodge Officer.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The proponent of Resolution 90-11 has proposed a sweeping revision of

which proposed legislation is presented to this Grand Lodge. Your Committee
on Policy and General Purposes views the Resolution to be, at best, impractical
and, at worst, unenforceable.
The first recommended change to be addressed by this Committee is the
requirement that where two or more pro~sals on the same subject are submitted to the Grand Lodge for consideration, the one receiving the lar~est
number of affirmative votes shall prevail and shall become the adopted legislation. My Brethren, we oppose this legislation for the following reason: As we
have previously stated, any legislative matter, or part thereof, that is not in
conflict with similar legislation, having received a legal majority vote, should not
be disenfranchised.

It is also proposed in the Resolution that Section 160 be amended to require

is our opinion that this Grand Lodge is blessed with some of the most dedicated

this fraternity, always with great compassion for the individual Mason, and
always within the framework of our Masonic law. So may it long continue.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to change the California Masonic

for the appointment of a Lodge Director of Ceremonies and Assistant Director

and five-sixths affirmative vote is required for adoption.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution no. 90-13 has been
referred. reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to clarify existing language in
respect to the investment of the funds of Grand Lodge and the Constituent
Lodges so as to leave no question that shares in mutual funds are among those
areas into which funds may be invested.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend the Ordinances and a five-sixths affirmative
vote is required for adoption.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
We understand the purpose of this Resolution to be the amendment of the
form of Sections 1292 and 2302, but not the substance. It clarifies the meaning
of those sections by updating one of the terms which they use.
As noted by the proponents, mutual funds have the advantages of diversification and professional management to an extent which would otherwise be
impossible for an individual investor. If the current terminology has deterred
any Lodge or Grand Lodge trustee from considering a mutual fund investment,
then the amendment is justified.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes"
vote.
The Committee on Investment:

We consider this Resolution to be merely a "housekeeping" one, to clarify
and update the language of the C.M.C. so as to remove an area of confusion.
The lan~age of the applicable portions of the C.M.C. now reads to allow
certain porttons of investment funds to be invested in "shares of Investment
Trusts". It was the feeling of the Investment Committee that the language, when
originally drafted and approved meant the shares in what we now regularly call
mutual funds. However, from time to time we have received questions on that
point indicating that some degree of confusion exists.
Several months ag,o the Investment Committee asked the Jurisprudence
Committee for a clarification on this point. Most Worshipful Don McCaw,
Chairman of the Jurisprudence Committee wrote indicatin~ the. Committee
agreed that the lan.guage, as it is now written, does indeed mclude shares in
mutual funds. However, there remains confusion, so we felt this Resolution was
in order so as to modify the language for all to read.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

257

Thus, the adoption of this Resolution will not in any way alter the meaning
of the C.M.C. nor expand or restrict how funds may now be invested. It will
merely make the language more modem and clarify a confusing point.
The Investment Committee recommends your "Yes" vote.
Resolution ADOPTED.

The Committee on Policy and Genera/ Pulposes:
Grand Lo~e has developed guidelines as parts of its Ordinances, separately applicable to mvestments of the funds of Grand Lodge and the Constituent
Lodges.
These conservative guidelines are the results of practical experiences and
expertise of professional, Masonic investment managers and have been approved by the Fraternity. They have provided limits of safety in the increasingly
complex field of investment. Experience has proven these guidelines have been
helpful and protective. Consequently, any changes or additions proposed
should be carefully considered.
Not all Masons having to do with the funds of Grand Lodge or of the
Constituent Lodges are capable in the complexities of fraternal fund investment.
We recognize, however, that the proponents or this Resolution are not only
successful investment managers in their personal lives, but are also effective
me mbers or the Grand Lodge Investment Committee. Whether because of the
analytic inabilities of members of our Committee to unde rstand the merits of
the proposals, or because of lack of substantiating information within the
Resolubon itself, we are not convinced that the proposed additions to our
Ordinances would be of benefit to Grand Lodge or to the Constituent Lodges.
We have received and considered information from outside the Committee,
both in favor and in opposition to the additions proposed in the Resolution.
Because of our inability to reach a conclusion on this matter, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes makes no recommendation to the Grand
.L odge.

The Committee on Investment:
Unlike the prior Resolution, this one is not just a "housekeeping" measure;
however, like Resolution 90-13, it does not deal with the need to bring our Grand
Lodge into the modern world in the investment arena, again a matter of

PRECLUDING NAMING A MASONIC TEMPLE OR
A ROOM OR AREA AFTER A LMNG PERSON
(90-15)

The proponent of this Resolution seeks to repeal Grand Master Channon's
Decision No. 89-2 and to preclude the naming of a ~e Room or other area
in a Masonic Temple or Lodge meeting place after a living person.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. & A . M. of California:
WHEREAS, in making Decision 89-2, Grand Master Channon correctly
pointed out that Section 2002 of the California Masonic Code does not address
the question of naming a room in a Masonic Temple after a living brother; and
WHEREAS, said Section 2002 protects the Craft from the peril of
memorializing a person, who, at some later date, loses his good standing with
the Craft and having a Lodge then placed in the position of memorialiZing a
person who is entirely undeserving of the honor; and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

263

Tht Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In 1989 Grand Master Channon ruled that it was proper to name a room
or area within a Masonic Temple in honor of a Brother Mason whether living
or deceased.
The Grand Master was aware of Section 2002 of the California Masonic
Code, which prohibits naming a Lodge for a living person. However, there are
occasions when a donation can rroperly be acknowledged by the use of a name.
Mo.st Lodges have a number o rooms and even if the main Lodge room itself
is named for a person , that does not mean that the Lodge will bear that name.
Grand Master Channon made such a distinction and we believe that the
distinction is valid as now annotated, Section 2002a California Masonic Code.

WHEREAS, the spirit of said Section 2002 also applies to the naming of a
room in a Masonic Temple and M asoory must be protected from this peril also.

Furthermore, we do not see that this decision imperils our fraternity. We
Masons must think positively toward the enrichment and betterment of Masonry. We should not be negative by assuming that the Brother so honored may
possibly at sometime in the future lose his Masonic Standing. If this should
poss_ibly happen there is nothing to prohibit the renaming of tfie room or area
at a later date.

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the California Masonic
Code be amended to read as follows:

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote
on this Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponent of Resolution No. 90-17 states that there is some confusion
concerning California Masonic Code Section 2049 which was prepared for
publication following the adoption of both Resolution 88-9 and Grand Master's
Recom.m endation No. 12 at the 1989 session of this Grand Lodge. The
proponent's Resolution, if adopted, would permit the sale, by Masonic orgaruzations, of alcoholic beverages in Masonic buildings or on Masonic properues.
It is not the prerogative of the Policy and General Purposes Committee to
interpret Masoruc Law, and since Section 2049 L'i the current law it will remain
in effect as stated in the Code, subject to the adoption of amendments or
changes to the law by proper delegates at this or future Grand Lodge sessions.
However, it is the ducy of this Committee to suggest Grand Lodge policy
to the delegates for their consideration.
Prior to the adoption of Section 2049 at the 1989 session of Grand Lodge
there had been numerous resolutions concerning the sale and/or use of alcoholic bevera~es by members of the Fratcrnicy while acting as members of the
several Masonic organizations. A special study committee prepared a lengthy
report which was submitted to the Grand Lodge at the 1988 session. The study
was authorized by then Grand Master Jack Levitt in an attempt to discover the
reasons behind the flurry of alcoholic beverage proposals and, hopefully, find
a reasonable means to liberalize the law to some degree.
That study committee learned that much of the desire to permit the use of
alcoholic beverages in Masonic buildings came from a real need by Lod~es and
Temple Associations to find new sources of revenue so as to maintain. their
properties in good fashion. The law, as it existed in 1988, prevented Masonic
organizations from renting their properties to non-Masonic groups who might
want to serve such bever~ges. A pr~e e~ple was that such property could
not be rented for wedding recepllOns if alcohol were to be served. That
deficiency was eliminated by Section 2049 which was adopted last year.
When your Committee on Policy and General Purposes reviewed Grand
Master Channon's Recommendation No. 12, it stated its opinion that the sale

Notwithstanding Past Grand Master Channon's detailed review of the

circumst~ces surrounding the adoption and printing of California Masonic

Code Section 2049, we recommend that the law remain as it is now written and
that you vote "NO" on proposed Resolution No. 90-17.

The Committee on Youth Orders:

The proponent seeks to allow constituent Lodges to sponsor and provide
financial support to youth activities whether or not the organization is sponsored
by a Lodge.

This Committee feels that such action would dilute the Masonic support
for our own Masonic affiliated Youth Groups. Furthermore, that such support
for other youth group activities may make our own groups feel slighted.
There are many DeMolay Chapters, Rainbow Assemblies and Job's
Dauw.iters Bethels that may have a soccer team, a basketball team or perhaps
a drill team that would appreciate the sponsorship and financial support of
Lodges, not necessarily their own sponsoring body.
We look further to the charter of this Committee, that we are to develop
effective Fraternal relations with DeMolay, Rainbow and Job's Daughters,
promote youth programs in the Lodges, and encourage Lod~e members to
provide adult leadership to local youth groups. For this CoDlmlttee to support
Resolution No. 90-20 would be in possible violation of our charter. We therefore
recommend a "No" vote.

LOWERING AGE OF ELIGIBILITY TO 18 YEARS
(90-25)

This Resolution seeks to amend the Ordinances and a five-sixths affirmative
vote is required for adoption.

The proeonents of this Resolution seek to reduce the required age for
membership tn the Fraternity from 21 years to 18 years.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M. of California:

Present Masonic Law prohibits a Mason who re.ceived his degrees subsequent to October 1953 from applying for membership in concordant Masonic
bodies until he has passed a proficiency examination in the Candidate's Lecture
of a Master Mason.

WHEREAS, the lawful age of consent in the United States bas been
established to be eighteen years; and

The proponents of Resolution No. 90-24 would change that date from
October 1953 to October 1990, thus removing that restriction from all Masons
who received their degrees prior to October 1990.

WHEREAS, several other Grand Jurisdictions have adopted eighteen years
as the lawful age for the degrees of Masonry; and
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge of California has expressed its desire for an
"accent on youth"; ~d

In r~nt year.s there ~ave. been several \>~oposals tC! e~ate or modi!Y
the restnel.Ion agamst applicauon to prereqws1te Masoruc bodies as stated U1
California Masonic Code Section 2635.

WHEREAS, with a declining member~p, the .a~option of thls R~lution
will provide for additional young men des.1.rous of JOuung our Fraterruty to do
so.

The restriction was adopted at a time when there were many applications
to Masonic Lodges for degrees. Further, it was believed. at the time Section
2635 was adopted, that it would encourage more candidates to pass the
proficiency of the third degree.

2636 of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:

In recent years the. number of applications to Lodges has declined. Further,
there is no evidence that the restrictions of present law have encouraged
members to pass the third degree proficiency. To the contrary, the restriction
has had a negative effect on applications to our concordant bodies. Your
Committee frequently has recommended that the restriction be removed.
However, the proposed Resolution does not remove the restriction, it
merely defers it to a new date. Consequently, the same problem will exist in the
years following October 1990 that exists now.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes reiterates its opinion that
the restriction caused by Section 2635 should be removed. Resolution No. 90-24
does not accomplish that purpose.

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the last sentence of Section
The Lodge cannot receive an application until the applicant has arrived
at the age of Wiealy eae eip.teen years.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The necessity of this Resolution hinges upon the meaning of the term "tiled
meet~, as used in that portion of California Masonic Code Section 2688 which
P.rohib1ts the .use of ritual ciphers in such meeting. The proponents apparently
view a gathenng of the officers of a Lodge to practice ntual as a tiled meeting
and thus urge the passage of this amendment. We, on the other hand, do not
believe that a practice session is a tiled meeting, and thus oppose this amendment.
Alth<?ugh the term "tiled meeting" is found in several places in our Code,
no~h~re !5 it defined. Howe~er, we ~ee no reason to give 1t an interpretation
which IS different from the plarn meanmg of the two words. Thus we understand
"tiled meeting" to be (1) a meeting at which (2) a tiler is on duty.
.APJ?lying the .first h.alf. of this de~tion, we do not believe that a practice
seSSJo.n IS a mee~ ~thin the mearung of our Cod.e. First, a gathering of
Masons, to practlce ntual or for any otlier purpose, IS not a meeting unless
If>dge is opened in one of the three degrees. We doubt that anyone spends the
~e to for_mally o~n and dose Lodge when the only reason for the gathering
JS to practlce the ritual, ao.d when no one is present but the officers and the
officer's coach. Second, our Code (Section 2550) requires that all members and
visitors record their names .in the tiler's register before entering any meeting.
We doubt that anyone registers attendance in the tiler's register at a ritual
praclfce. ~~ if a pract.ie:e. sessio.n is a meeting, then it is a special meeting.
Yet,~ descnbmg the a~vi.ttes which may properly be conducted at a special
meetmg, our Code (Sect10n 2042) does not mention the practicing of ritual.
While the list in that Section is not all-inclusive, the omission is evidence that
practice sessions are not meetings within the meaning of the Code.
The second element of the definition is that a tiler must be on duty. While
a practice of ritual must obviously be conducted in a place which is free from
eaves.droppers, ~care n<;>t aware of any requirements that a guard, in the person
of a tiler, be stattoned without the door.

!-n short~ w~ ~nstrue the term "tiled meeting" as a short-had for "stated or
s~ meetmg . Smee '!'e dou~t that practice sessions are typically conducted
~ either stated or speoal meetmgs, we believe that the proposed amendment
~ unnea:ssary. F~hermore, to the extent that it implies that a practice session
IS a special ~eetmg, wi.th all of the accompanying formalities which a special
meetmg entails, we believe that the amendment would lead to confusion and
would De a disincentive to regular practices by our officer corps.

For these reasons, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Ritual:
Since the approval of cipher rituals in 1988 the Ritual Committee has
resisted their use at ritual l>ractices and schools of instruction. Our reluctance
was based on a fear that therr presence would be disruptive and counter-prod uctive, particularly since they contained so many errors.

Inseectors' Conferences . With that experience, and with corrected ciphers now
available, our initial response to this Resolution was to recommend a "Yes" vote.

which meet reqwrements of our Ordinances and the approval of the Grand
Master, may, if they wish, make life membership programs effective. They
provide that by making one appropriate lump sum payment, a member could

'?c exempt from paying further Lodge dues for life. The minimum amount of
life membership payment is now $250 and is calculated from a base of$12 annual
membership dues. The minimum payment changes proportionately with the

304

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Lodge's current dues. Thus, $24 membership dues would require a $500 minimum lump sum payment, and $36 dues at least $750.
This Committee reiterates its previous stated position that it views the
general concept of Life Membership with favor as possible long term financial
help for many of our Lodges. Potential benefits grow out of the fact that the Life
Membership fees become part of a permanent, separate "Life" fund, earnings
from which can be used for operating expenses and continue indefinitely beyond
the date of the participating members' deaths.

In Lodges where Life Membership resolutions have been adopted, the
minimum payments required are now uniformly applicable to all interested
members regardless of their differing ages.
The Life Membership Plan proposed as an alternative by this Resolution
provides that the calculation factor for minimum required lump sum payments
for members under age 49 remain the same. Such payments would thereafter
decline by bracketed scale as the ages of newly participating members increase.
Thus a new participant who is 60 years of age and whose Lodge dues are
$40, might be applying the scale of this proposal purchase a life membership for
$5(i0. This amount is the equivalent of Lodge dues he would have ,P.aid at $40
until age 74. This amount when invested by the Lodge as part of its Life" fund,
at even a modest, simple interest of7.5%, would produce $42 annual income in
lieu of his $40 dues.
Even though this plan does make it more difficult for a younger member
than an older one to purchase a Lodge membership, younger participants have
greater life expectancy.
We believe that adoption of this Resolution will encourage more older
members to participate in life membership plans because the purchase prices
are more equitable. Further, such participation will benefit the Lodges in both
their long and short term financial situations.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes•
vote.
Resolution HELD OVER.

REPORT OF THE COMMITIEE ON
HISTORIC SITES AND BUILDINGS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M. of California:
The Historic Sites and Building.s Committee was created by action taken
at the 1989 Grand Lodge Communication which consolidated the Cemetery,
Columbia Temple, Old Masonic Hall in Los An~eles and Quitman Temple
Committees into one. The new Committee contmues to be responsible for

316

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

.

preserving, maintaining and improving the various sites under its care. C-Ontinuity was provided by having most of the former separate Committee members
continue to serve on the consolidated one.
Four cemeteries, Columbia, Jamestown, Michigan Bluff and Fiddletawn
became the responsibility of Grand Lodge when the Lodges which had started
them either gave up their charters or had them revoked, or consolidated with
other Lodges. Peter Lassens' gravesite near Susanville is cared for by virtue of
the fact that he was a Mason of renown. Our responsibility is to maintain each
of the sites to a standard which is comparable to the private or community
cemeteries in their respective areas. I am pleased to report that this has been
done, or exceeded in every instance.
Care of these sites consists of mowing the natural grasses, the spraying of
weeds, tree trimming, raking leaves, repair and restoration of headstones,
leve~ walkways and the repair and paintin~ of fences. There have been no
recent mterments in the above listed cemeteries.
Fallbrook Masonic Cemetery is an active, operating cemetery doing approximately 100 interments per year. It is managed by a Board of Directors
which is separate from this Committee, has endowment care funds as required
by the State of California for operating cemeteries and has full time help to
maintain it. No Grand Lodge funds are required for its operation or maintenance. It was recommended to the Grand Master this past February and
restated here that this cemetery should not be under the Jurisdiction of this
Committee.
The three Temples overseen by this Committee are Columbia, Quitman
and the Old Masoruc Hall in Los Angeles. All are located within State Parks.
Columbia and Quitman Temples are recreations of the original Temples.
Columbia is constructed of brick while Quitman is of wood. Both are extremely
well cared for and their appearance is outstanding. Of the three Temples,
Columbia is probably seen by more visitors annually than the others. It is located
off Highway 49 just outside of Sonora.
Quitman Temple, located at the Malakoff Diggins' is somewhat off the
beaten path and consequently does not receive the public visitation that Columbia Temple does. This is unfortunate because Quitman is also an excellent
recreation of a Masonic Temple of the late 1800's.
The Old Masonic Hall in Los Angeles is not a recreation, but is the original
two-story structure that was built in 1858. Considering its age, it is in excellent
condition. Unfortunately, it is located in a part of Los Angeles which makes the
use of the Temple very difficult. (ie: Parking and a not very safe part of the city
to be in after dark.) The cWTent tenant, Plaza de Los Angeles Lodge No. 814
is in the process of seeking consolidation with another Lodge and when they
leave, the future of the buifding will bear considerable scrutiny and will be the
primary problem to be faced in 1991.

REPORT OF THE COMMITI'EE ON
LODGE RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The Masonic Lodge and Resources Development Committee is pleased to
present the following Annual Report and recommendations for the 1989 - 1990
Masonic year.
•
•

There are 15 C~mmittee members presently serving on the
Resources Committee.
We a:1eet ~th a full Committee on a quarterly basis. We hold two
meetmgs m Northern California and two in Southern California.
One Northern meeting is held during Grand .L odge week. Our
annual budget is $6,500.

3. Our . Committee was responsible for reviewing and summarizing
approXlDlately 1,000 responses to the "Under 45" membership opinion
survey. The questionnaires were equally distributed to Committee
members. Each Committeeman became well informed on the responses for an overall Committee evaluation. These responses were
thoroughly discussed and a prior report mailed to you summarizing the
recorded responses. As a result of the questionnaire, we prepared the
attached letter of recommendations dated March 27, 1990, for consideration and recording at this Grand Lodge proceedings. Major
recommendations included:
a. A California and Hawaii computer network for mailings
should be considered for sojourners, in order to invite them
and encourage attendance at the local Lodge where they now
•
reside.
b. We suggest that Grand Lodge. make it mandatory for Senior
Wardens lo prepare an annual plan and budget, which must
then be approved by the Lodge membe rship prior to his
advancement to Master -- in order lo encourage sound fiscal
management and planned Lodge activities.
c. Sojourners should only have to show a paid-up dues card in
order to visit another Lodge.
d. We suggest the rules on how to invite non-Masons into
Masonry be relaxed.
e. Change the name of Laymen's Night.
f. A financial incentive (initiation fee reduction) should be
considered for past DeMolay members to join a Masonic
Lodge before their 21st to 25th birthday. This incentive might
also be expanded to other young men m the same age group
category.
