GRAND WOGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Reflections
The Masonic Homes Endowment Fund fiscal year of 1989 - 1990 was
indeed a memorable one. One that all Masons of California can be justifiably
proud. The programs that were instituted twolears ago to increase the awareness of the Masonic Homes in the members o our Fraternity is indeed paying
off.
The presentation of the book "The Greatest of These is Charity" has been
widely accepted as one of the great enlightenments where the Entered Apprentice is made aware of our primary Masonic charity early in his Masonic career.
Even some of the "sideliners" are showing interest in their requests as to where
they can procure a copy of the book.
The response to the Masonic H ome Lapel Pin and the Appreciation
Certificates has far exceeded our expectations in terms of the numbers
presented. New pins and certificates will be available in 1990 - 1991.
This past year was the first year without Hawaii as a part of our Grand
Lodge and of course the number of Masons belonging to our jurisdiction
decreased. We now have 145,319, a loss of8,424 members.
However, there were many pluses - the total dollars contributed through
the Lodges was up even more than when Hawaii was a part of our Grand Lodge
- the dollars per contributor as well as the dollars per member increased
significantly - even the percent of the Lodges achieving Honor Roll status
increased over the previous year.
There a:re few concerns even with all the good things. We are still not able
to increase the participation in the Endowment Fund program, and two of the
Divisions bad significant reductions in their contributions. There were five
Lodges that did not contribute anything and there were many which had a very
low fevel of participation. Somehow we must find a way to reach those who do
not r,articipate. We do not understand why Divisions II and m dropped so
significantly in their total contributions this past year.
We are pleased to report that the average contribution per contributor
increased over 8 r,.ercent to $20.35 per contributor. It is difficult to assess, or
evaluate the significance of the number of contributors. Some Lodges show
many more contributors than members aod others show large contributions and
indicate none or a low number of contributors. It may be the manner that we
record the information. The real important thing is that the average contribution
per member increased to $9.92 per member from $9.27 for the prior year and
that the total dollars increased by almost 3 %.

Planning for the Future
The Individual Contribution Incentive Program got off to a very rocky start
in that we had logistic problems that we did not foresee. The "l Gave" buttons
were late in delivery and when they did arrive the distnbution became very
cumbersome. This year we have chan~ed to buttons to "Give in 1991" and were
mailed to all Lodges in time for their mclusion in their 1991 dues envelopes. It
is hoped that these reminders will encourage our non-giver to join in on the
personal satisfaction of giving to help someone less fortunate.

Your Endowment Board must find a better way to record the number of
contributors without increasing the work load of the Secretaries of the Lod~es.
Your Endowment Board has looked into a new Endowment Fund Receipt.
When current supplies of the existing Endowment Funds Receipts are exhausted, we will have a new receipt that will have an added copy that will be for
the Endowment Board. Using pressure sensitive paper, getting an added copy
will not cause the Secretary any added work.

Epilogue

Our sincere and grateful thanks to the Grand Master, Sam M. Pavlovich,
and to the Grand Lodge Officers, Board Members and Committeemen who
have been supportive of the Endowment ~r<?~am. We also wish to thank the
Masters, Wardens, Secretaries and expecially the Lodge Endowment Fund
Chairmen for their efforts in furthering this worthy program.
We also extend a special thanks to the 70,834 Brothers who, through their
continued generosity, contributed over one million four hundred thousand
dollars to the Endowment Fund during this fiscal year.
We appreciate the splendid assistance and support we have received from
the Masoruc Homes Board of Trustees, the Grand Secretary's office, under the
leadership of the Grand Secretary, Robert A. Klinger, and the staff of the Grand
Lodge office.
Once again I wish to offer my personal thanks to every Homes Endowment
Board member for their dedication and devotion in the surport extended to me
during this past year as your Chairman. No other group o people can measuce
up to the contributions made by the members of the Endowment Board. With
all the new demands presented to them, they have responded with vigor and
enthusiasm and their response was most gratifying. It is the great people of the
Endowment Board who work so diligently that ensures the success of our
program. My special thanks to the members that have reached tenure of nine
or more years of service to the Homes. Your service will be missed.
Respectfully submitted,
John M. (Jack) Palmer, Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITI'EE ON
MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M. of California:
The Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus is pleased to submit its Annual
Report on the operations and conditions of the seventeen Masonic Service
Bureaus for the year ending June 30, 1990. The Committee is in its 63rd year.
Right Worshi&ful Ronald A. Sherod, Deputr Grand Master, was appointed
liaison officer to e Committee and we appreciate his support and assistance
during the year.

This Committee is well aware of its responsibility in oversee~d directing the operation of the various Bureaus m a uniform manner.
e Service
Bureaus assist sojourners, their widows and orphans; operate blood banks;
arrange and conduct funerals for deceased Masons; make investigations; assist
~ pr~_ssing ~I?plicati.ons for the two Masonic Ho~es an~ Ho~es in other
JurtSdictlons; visit the stck and promote fraternal relations with so1ourners.
Committee Members
We were sorry to acceaht the resignation of Worshipful Merrill R. Shelley,
who stepped down for he th reasons. He had served on the Committee with
distinction since 1985. Worshipful Shelley, a member of Ojai Lodge No. 663,
was replaced by Worshi8ful Ray Rookard, who had reviously rerformed
excellent service on the ommittee. He is a member o Acalanes ellowship
Lodge No. 480.
Executive Secretaries
Clyde Hubbell, Executive Secretllh of the Masonic Service Bureau of San
Gabriel Valley, res:r,ed because of ill ealth. He was replaced by Worshipful
Bill Carnot. We wis Worshipful Carnot all the best in his new position.

E. Charles Lamberson rested as Executive Secretary of the Masonic

Charles L. Hart, who took over the reins of

Meetings
The Committee held four meetings during the year. One was held on the
first two days of Grand Lodge week, Monda(; and Tuesday, October 9th and
10th. In addition, a booth was manned on " " Floor where information was
passed out and a film was shown concerning our new ho~ital visitation program
under the aegis of the Masonic Service Association of e United States.

A regional meeting was held in Oakland on February 10, 1990 with Committee members plus 16 members and guests of the Bureaus fr<;>m Northern
California in attendance. Bureau activities and reports were discussed and
discussion was bad on various problems confronting the Bureaus.

A regional meeting was held in Los Angeles on March 24, 199!J wi!h
Committee members plus 25 members and guests from Southern Califorrua
Bureaus attending. Guests included Worshipful William Widenham, a former
member of the Committee. We were privileged to have as our guest speaker
Very Worshipful Robert A. Klinger, Grand Secretary, who spoke on se~eral
topics of current interest. We were also privileged to bear from Most Worhs1pful
Thomas Dougherty, P.G.M., New Jersey who is the Dir~ctor of Hospital
Visitation of the Masonic Service Association of the Uruted States. Most
Worshipful Dougherty gave a most interesting presentation on the hospit~
visitation program and brought us up to date on the progress of the program m
the various VA Hospitals in California and elsewhere.

Operating Expenses

On Wednesday, June 13, 1990, four members of the Committ~e met. in
Pasadena to review the proposed budgets of the seventeen Masoruc Semce
Bureaus. The Committee also reviewed its own budget for the 1990 - 1991
Masonic year. The Pasadena Scottish Rite graciously provided the facilities and
coffee for our meeting.

Total cost of operating the seventeen Bureaus for the year ending June 30,
1990 amounted to $170,986.44. Fixed expenses were $112,895.37; telephone,
printing and postage were $16,971.27 and taxes were $9,878.35. Some Executive
Secretaries receive a modest salary while others receive none. A few choose to
receive mileage only.

After each of the above meetings, a short business meeting of the Committee was held to discuss items of immediate import.

MSA Hospital Visitation Program

Taxes
All Bureaus filed the required information with the Internal Revenue
Service and with the State Franchise Tax Board. Bureaus required to fiJe tax
returns did so and filed them on time.
Bush Masonic Relief Fund
The Bush Masonic Relief provides operating funds for the five Bureaus
located in the greater Los Angeles area. The contributions from this fund
amounted to more than 68% of the total income for the seventeen Bureaus and
we appreciate this generous contribution for operations in the greater Los
Angeles area.
Several of our Bureaus operate blood banks for the benefit of California
Masons and their families as well as for sojourners. One thousand forty-three
units of blood were donated during the year and 473 units were released to
provide this important life support to our members, their families and to
sojourners. In addition, $2,787.70 in cash ("green blood") was donated to the
San Francisco Bureau and $155.94 to the Fresno Bureau in lieu of actual blood
donations.
Uniform Compacts

At the 140th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge we began the
new hosrital visitation program under the auspices of the Masonic Service
Association of tbt! United States. Programs have been established at four
Veterans' Administration Hospitals; Wadsworth, under the direction of
Brother Arthur Rumsey; Sawtelle, under Brother Royal Dano; Sepulveda,
under Brother DeMay H. "Dee" White; and San Diego, under Brother
Theodore E. Gibbon, who also serves as Master of Joseph L. Shell Daylight
Lodge No. 837. A pro~am is in the beginning states at the VA Hospital in Long
Beach and should be m full swing soon. Members of six Lodges in the area are
already visiting there. We are in the planning stages of starting programs at
Hospitals in Northern California as well.
Conclusions
Special appreciation and thanks are expressed to the Grand Master, Most
Worshipful Sam M. Pavlovich, and his Grand Lodge office staff for their
continued support and to the Deputy Grand Master, Right Worshipful Ronald
A. Sherod, for his assistance as our liaison officer. We also thank the Grand
Secretary, Very Worshipful Robert A. Klinger, who spoke to us at our Los
Angeles meeting and who provided continuing help throughout the year.

358

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDlNG S OF THE

Appreciation is also expressed to the Presidents, officers and representatives of all Bureaus in this Grand Jurisdiction for their great and continued
interest .i n and devotion to the activities of the various Bureaus and for their
help to our sojourning Brethren and their families.
Our Executive Secretaries deserve special note as they are in the forefront
of our fraternal and charitable business and are on call every day and night of
the year. These Brethren are the backbone of our Bureaus and to each we
express our deep and abiding appreciation for their work.
The Committee budget during the past year was sufficient for us to function
properly and economically and a budget of $3, 107.00 has been approved for the
coming year.
Respectfully submitted,
A Bruce Ivie, Chainnan

Grand Lodge or New Jersey 1989 - Membership 52,595 - Loss 2,197

Grand Lodge or Vermont 1988- Membe.r ship 11,135 - Loss U3

Much of the Grand Master's term in office was taken up dealing with the
issue of perceived discrimination in voting of new members by the Shrine in New
Jersey. The Grand Master attempted to work the problem with the Shrine
leadership, but meeting with resistance, was forced to issue edicts barring New
Jersey Masons from participating in Shrine activities.

!he. offer~ use or distribution of alcoholic beverages is granted by a
special dispensation from the Grand Master. Last year, forty-two dispensations
were issued to various Masonic bodies.

Grand Lodge or Oklahoma 1988 - Membership 49,258 - Loss 1,981

The Grand Master ruled that it was not a violation of the Masonic Code
for a Mason running for political office to include in a political ad the fact that
he is a Mason.

The Grand Lodge has 2,538 Perpetual Members and 100 memorial Perpetual Members with $863,477 in the Trust Fund. Memorial Perpetual memberships are obtained in the name of the deceased Master Mason for $150.00
by the spouse or others. At the Grand Lodge Communication a Resolution was
proeosed to lower minimum age for membership to those in the Armed Services
to mneteen years.
Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania 1988 - Membership 183,404 - Loss 6~57
All Grand Lodge Officers are titled "Right Worshipful" and the Grand
Master serves two years. As Pennsylvania has quarterly Grand Lodge meetings,
a report was presented at each on the progress of the "Solomon 11" project.
Although no specific information regarding the contents were given, the main
thrust seems to be reducing suspensions and demits through Masonic education
programs, and encouraging new membership through public information displays at outside events.

Grand Lodge or Tennessee 1989 - Membership 87-566 - Loss 1,093

Due to declining membership and rising costs, an increase of $1.00 to the
per capita was requested. The increase was not approved.
Grand Lodge of Wisconsin 1989 - Membership 30,417 - Loss 1,259
Resolution proposed to authorize Grand Lodge Trustees to lend Grand
Lodge funds to constituent Lodges at a rate of equal interest to the money
marICet rates.
Grand Lodge or Wyoming 1989 - Membership 8,541- Loss 332
<;1rand. Mast~r 1 Most Worshipful Charles H. Moore, and others attended a
meehng with William L . Hunter, Grand Master of Prince Hall Masons in
Colorado, Utah and Wyoming, in Denver at the request of Colorado Grand
Master, Most Worshipful Dwight Hamilton.

Grand Lodge of Utah 1989 - Membership 3,751 - Loss 106
Proficiency requirements for Masters-elect do not include memorization
of the lectures of the three degrees. Grand Lodge produces official ciphers and
lowered the price to $10.00 to encourage distribution to a larger number of
members in good standing. Grand Lodge per capita stands at $11.00 (steady
since 1986).

The Grand Lodge voted to recognize the new Grand Lodge of Hawaii and
the Grand Orient of Italy.
The Grand Lodge grants Honorary Membership to all Distinguished
Guests attending their Annual Communication.
Grand Lodge of Alberta 1988

Due to an inventory of Past Grand Master's jewels donated back from
deceased Past Grand Masters, the Board of Trustees decided that instead of
purchasing a new jewel each year, a jewel from inventory will be loaned for life
to each new Past Grand Master.
Grand Lodge of Vermont 1990 - Membership 10,878 - Gain 257

As of Dece~ber 31,.1988, the Grand Lodge had 157 Lodges, 155 Chartered
and 2 Under Dispensat10n. Three hundred nine Master Mason and 136 Past
Master certificates were issued. In 1988 the membership went from 12,713 to
12,234 for a net loss of 479.

Grand Lodge of India 1989

An important action by Grand Lodge Trustees was the inco.rpora~on of

the "Masonic Charities of Vermont". It will be the instrument for combating
substance abuse among youn~ children. The Grand Lodge Committee for the
handicapped makes and provides specialized eating utensils for any (Masonic
or non-Masonic) handicapped person. The Grand Master stated that Grand
Lodge Officers should conllnue to make public appearances in regalia to bring
the Fraternity and its good works to the attention of the uninitiated.

The Grand Lodge has 274 Lodges which is an increase of 4 Lodges and has
~4,568 members which is an increase of about 400 members. The Grand Lodge
as proceeding with plans to build a central Masonic hospital in Delhi.

The Minnesota Mason • October 1989

In 1989 there were 1,302 newly raised Master Masons while only 1,1
1988, an increase of 10.5%.

The Grand Master's Festival bas raised over 250,000 pounds, to establish
the Freemasons of Ireland Medical Research Fund. Grand Lodge has a "St.
John's Day Charity Collection" which is used for special needs outside of
Ireland. One thousand pounds was raised from the Grand Master's newly
instituted "Discretionary Fund" to go to those injured in the fighting and unrest
in Romania.
Grand Lodge of New Brunswick 1989

The Grand Lodge has experienced a net loss in membership of 4%.
1986 - 7,056

1987 - 6,958

371

1988 - 6,770

In 1980, Minnesota Masonry started a state-wide program to aid youth
suffering from diabetes. To date, 70% of Lodges have participated in the
placement of blood glucose meters in schools. Lodges will be asked to provide
a $10.00 donation per meter supervisors attending technical updates from
schools located in a Lodge's territory.
The Minnesota Mason - December 1989

A Resolution was passed at Grand Lodge which makes it possible to
lawfully ask a man if he would like to be a Mason. He can only be asked once,
and be allowed to make up his own mind. He can be told "I thiDk you would be
a good Mason and I will sign your petition if you want to join".
The Minnesota Mason • February 1990

No new Lodges were constituted nor were any closed. The Grand Master
noted in his State of the Craft message that during his many visits lo the various
Lodges, that the Grand Officers out-numbered the Lodge members.

The Grand Lodge has a program whereby the Grand Lodge will pay half
of the cost of running an ad in the local newspaper. The program, called Co-op
Advertising, has proved helpful to the Lodges.

Grand Lodge Newsletter of Illinois • May 1990

The Minnesota Mason ·June 1990

The Grand Master's Message mentioned that many requests for Lodge
mergers were being received, but that he had decided to hold them without
action. He charged the District Deputy Grand Masters with the task of turning
these Lodges healthy once more.

The Grand Master asked all Brethren to attend the house of their worship
on the weekend of June 22-24. The effort was to celebrate St. John's Day and
provide a positive example of Freemasonry. A listing was included of all Grand
Officers and the addresses of respective churches, so that any Brother could
join them in wors~p.

Grand Lodge Bulletin of Iowa • March 1990

The Grand Lodge has started a new program to improve their public image.
Two billboards were posted in each six metropolitan areas across the State. The
billboards have a square and compass and say "The Fraternity That
Cares...Masonic Lodges of Iowa".
Grand Lodge Bulletin of Iowa - June 1990

The Grand Master reports that there is excellent progress in the Grand
Lodge Video Project. The first video, "Opening the Doors of Freemasonry", is
being used by Lodges at Friendship Nights. The second video covers the history
of Masonry and the third is designed to be shown to the newly initiated Entered
Apprentice.

Texas Mason • Winter 1989
In the Winter of 1989, Resolutions introduced were (1) Masonic offense to
dese<:rate the _American Flag, (2) allow ball~~ on affiliations during Stated
Meetmg at which read, (3) allow Stated Meetmgs m Entered Apprentice degree
and make all Entered Apprentices and Fellowcrafts pay dues.
Texas Mason • Spring 1990

The Grand Master has approved the admission of non-Masonic children
to the Masonic Home and School. He has also recognized the Iotemational
Order.of Job's Daughters, leading to the institution of Bethel No. 1 in San
Antoruo.
The Varginia Masonic Herald· July 1989

The G.rand Master is leading a crusade to provide care for helpless children
by requestmg all Masons lo donate $10.00 or more to a fund he has established
for this purpose.

Masons and their families at no charge. The prosram is being developed by Sinai

Foundation has supported a Masonic Diagnostic and Treatment Center at the

emergency treatment and out-patient services.

The Committee has been more aggressive in calling upon the administrative
arm of the Grand Lodge, the Inspectors, to enforce the provisions of the
California Masonic Code as they relate to the Temple Associations within their
various administrative districts.
Financial Reporting
The most recent reports to the Grand Lodge from the Temple Associations
indicates that the financial health of many of the Temple Boards is ailin~. Of
concern, the decline in the number of tenants renting the Temple Associations'
building space on an on-going basis as a result of mergers, dwindling numbers
of youth and ladies groups and fewer Lodges as tenants. Recent changes in the
Masonic Law on outside rentals bas not yet bad a full impact on the Temple
Associations. This development will be monitored closely in 1990-1991 and
reported to you next year.
Committee Reorganization
The Committee has implemented many of the suggestions from the 19891990 year; members have been assigned by territory in the state, and are now
establishing relations with the Lodges, Temple Associations and Inspectors in
their respective areas. The responses of the Committee to requests for authority
to perform work in under a value of $25,000 has been delegated to the local
Committeemen; the result has been improved review and speedier decisions for
the Temple Associations.

The Committee on Temple Properties is pleased to submit the following
annual report of its activities for the 1989-1990 Masonic Year:
Uniform By-laws
A~ain this was the number one subject of the inquiries to our members and

for acttvities of the members in working with the Temple Boards. Compliance
with the California Masonic Code, Sections 2304 and 2305, on the use of the
"Uniform By-Laws" and the return of funds above those necessary to operate
the Temples have been foremost in our efforts.

In 1983, the COmmittee issued its "Handbook," which has been in use as a
guide to the Lodges and Temples throughout the state. In 1990, the revision of
the "Handbook" was undertaken. While It is not now complete, it has areas still
undergoing revision at this session, it should be ready for the 1991 Temple
Properties workshop for all of the Temple Associations to secure.
Workload
The Committee expected to see a reduced workload as a result of the
actions at the 1989 session of the Grand Lodge. This bas yet to materialize, the
1990 workload was as great as in preceding years:
37 requests were received by the Committee for approval of alterations,
addillons, acquisitions or capital expenditures;
10 were kept open as the Temples needed furhter technical assistance
on their requests;
26 were approved by the Committee as presented by the Temple
Associations;

ON U.S. CONSTITUfION OBSERVANCE

This year, as in 1989 and with the Grand Master's permission, I appointed
Maurice R. Crosby as Vice-Chairman. Due to the size of the state, this appointment has greatly improved the efficiency of the Committee, giving us leadership
in both the northern and southern parts of the state.
All of the Leadership Workshops during the last year had a U.S. Consti~
tion Observance booth staffed by members of this hard-working Committee.
This active year was also punctuated by three Committee meetings; one in San
Francisco, one in Alameda, and one in Arcadia. Ideas on different programs
throughout the state were exchanged and discussed. We tried to impress upon
the Lodges the need to start planning early and the need to invite the public to
their observations. Grand Master Pavlovich declared September as U.S. Constitution Oservance Month.
Attendance at most programs increased again this year, mainly because of
the fme programs presented throughout the state. Nevada City, for the twentieth
time, had a parade; San Diego a program in Balboa Park; El Segundo are

program with good attendance. ~es held family nights and sI>ecial programs

in other facets of Masonry, particularly in the Shrine Hospitals. The twenty-six

thank them for their efforts.

Grand Chapter Order of Eastern Star

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A .M. of California:
The 1990 Grand Master's theme, "Visions of the 90's --Think Young, Think
Tomorrow," again lent itself to the general purposes of the Committee on Youth
Orders, which still remains two-fold.

Job's Daughters Grand Guardian Council
Northern California DeMolay Convention
Southern California DeMolay Conclave

To develop effective Fraternal relations with the members and adult
leaders of the three Youth Orders and to promote the increase of yo~th
progi:ams in the Lodges, as well as to encourage the Lodge members to provtde
additional adult leadership to their local youth groups.

California Grand Assembly, Internationa l Order of Rainbow
for Girls
California Grand Bethel, Internationa l Order of Job's
Daughters

This latter purpose continues to frustrate your Committee as well as the
existing adult leaders. Last year we reported to you that current youth order
membership had declined from 30,000 to 10,000 in the last twenty years. We are
sorry to report to you, my Brethren, that this trend bas n ot changed.
There is HOPE howeve r, in that two of the three Youth Organization s have
reported that they experienced the smallest decline ever in many years. HOPE
is an .interes~ word, in our degr.ees as.well as th~ sacred volume, we are taught
that Ji along with FAITH mean little without th err partner CHARITY.
Brethren, the Youth Groups need your charity. Not in monetary terms, but
in your voluntary giving of time, understandin g and patience.
There are Assemblies, Bethels and Chapters which closed th.is past year -not for the lack of membership but for the lack of a sufficient number of adult
volunteers. Your Committee on Youth Orde rs asks that each member of the
Grand Lodge here today, return to your Temples and seek out a Rainbow
Mother Advisor, or Job's Bethel Guardian or DeMolay Chapter Dad and
repeat the following four words, "HOW CAN I HELP?"
These people will know that you as Masters and Wardens cannot devote
much more of your time than you already have, however, they also know that
you are best suited to know who in your Lodge can spare additional time.
Perhaps the newest raised Master Mason in your Lodge could avail himself.
Think about it Brethren! At the 1989 Annual Communicat ion, our Grand
Secretary reported to you that 1,284 men were raised to the degree of Master
Mason. If each of them had committed to just one year of youth service along
with the responsibilit y of fmding a successor, the Youth Groups could have
more than.doubled their current adult leadership. Moreover, many Masons who
have served the Youth Orders tirelessly for years, could have rested just a bit,
returned to their Lodges and enjoyed renewed fellowship as well as a change
of pace.

your Grand Lodge at the following events:

Grand Wardens were individually introduced and installed. The Deputy Gran
d.Master was then duly installed. Brother Winterton rendered his second selection, prior to a prayer offered to the Great Architect of the Universe by the
Grand Master-elect, as he knelt at the altar.
The Grand Master was then installed in due and ancient form and saluted
by the Brethren present with Public Grand Honors.
The newly installed Grand Master was pleased to welcome all in attendance
and introduced various groups who had come for the occasion.
Grand Master Sherod then introduced his wife, Terry, and other members
of his family, following which, he requestd all the newly installed Grand Lodge
officers to introduce the members of their families who were in attendance.

Pin to Junior Past Grand Master Sam M. Pavlovich; a Certificate, vouching for
his service to the Craft was presented by Past Grand Master Roy J. Henville,
and a Past Grand Master's Apron was presented by Past Grand Master Vernon
L. Gordon.
Persida Pavlovich, wife of the now Junior Past Grand Master Sam M.
Pavlovich, was escorted to the East where Past Grand Master Jack R. Levitt
presented here with a gift on behalf of the Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master invited all in attendance to a reception to be held in the
Exhibit Hall of the Memorial Temple. Adjournment was at 4:40 P.M. with
Grand Lodge to be formally closed following the reception.

balance for the years then ended . These financial statements are the responsibility of the Grand Lodge's
manageme nt. Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on o ur audir.
We conducted o ur a ud it in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those standards
require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial
statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes exa mining, on a test basis, evidence
supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An audit also includes assessing the
accounting principles used and significant estimates made by manRgement, as well as evaluating the
overall financial stattment presentation . We believe that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our
opinion.
In our opinion, the financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all materials respects,
the financial position of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the state of
California at June 30, 1990 and 1989 and the results of its operations and changes in fund balance for
the years then ended in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles.
Our audit was made for the purpose of fo rming an o pinion on the basic financ ial statements taken

NOTE I - SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:

f'IOTE 3 - PENSION PLAN:

Method of Accountjn&:
The financial statements of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California have been prepared on the accrual basis of accounting.

The Temple, Grand lodge and component organiiations and Masonic Homes contribute to
the California Masonic Retirement Plan for the benefit of eligible employees. Details to the plan
are contained in Note .5 to the financial statemems of the Masonic Homes of California.
Pension expense of the Grand Lodge charged to operations in 1990 and 1989 was $71,224 and
$211 ,911. respectively.

Revenµe Recognition:
Contributions and per-capita revenue from lodges are recognized as income on their
assessment date , June 30.

f'IOTE 4 - FEDERAL AND STATE INCOME TAXES:
The Grand Lodge is exempt f rom federal and s tate income taxes.

lnve51me01s:
Investments in marketable securities are stated at fair market value. Gains or losses that res ult
from sales or market nuctuations are recognized in t he period such sales or nuctuations occur.
Fyrnj!Yre Eayjoment and lmorovements:
Furniture, equipment and improvements are recorded at cost. and are depreciated on the
straight-line method over estimated useful lives of three to twenty-five years.

NOTES - EQUIPMENT CAPITAL LEASE:
The Grand Lodge purchased a copy machine under a capital lease expiring in 1993. The
equipment is capitalized at the present value of the min imum lease pa yments. The equipment is
depreciated over its lease term, which is shorter than its estima ted productive life. Depreciat ion
of the equipment under the cap ital lease was $4,740 in 1990 and S4, 737 in 1989 and is included in
depreciation expense.

Col!ectjblcs:
The Grand Lodge owns a collection of jewelry and other objects, most of which have
historical significance. The jewelry collection is used in Lodge ceremonies. and the other items are
displayed in the Temple Museum.

collectibles as revenue when received. Accessions and deaccessions during 1990 and 1989 were not

NOTE 6 - BEQUEST:
In 1990, the Grand l odge received $370,31 7 from the Estate of Jack I. MacKechnie. Mr.
MacKechnie's Will provides that the income, but not the principal, shall be used to provide
scholarships to accredited universities and colleges for need y high school graduates of proven
outstanding athletic ability. The Grand Lodge's tax exempt status does not provide fo r the granting
of scholarships to the public a t large and at June 30, 1990 legal proceedings were in process to give
effec t to the transfer of the Bequest to the Masonic Foundation for administration. The Beque.st
has earned interest of $ 2,367 through June 30, 1990.
l'IOTE 7 - EARTHQUAKE RELIEF FUND RAISI NG:
During 1990, the Grand Lodge raised $93,009 in contributions from its membership for
earthquake relief. Earthquake relief program expenditures totaled S26,057, resulting in an
unexpended fund balance of $66,9.52.

We have audited the accompan y ing balance shee.ts of the Masonic Homes of California, a California
nonprofit corporation, at June 30, 1990 and 1989, and the related statements of support, revenue and
expenses and c hanges in fund balances for the years then ended. These financial statements are the

financial statements based on our audits.
We conducted our audits in accordance with generall y accepted auditing standards. Those sta ndards
require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance abo ut whether the financial
statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes examining, on a test basis, e vidence
supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An audit also incl udes assessing the
accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management, as well as ev aluating the overall
financial statement presentation. We believe that our audits provide a reasonable basis for our opinion.

MILLIONS

Masonic Homes of California is a non-profit California Corporation administering 1 home
for adults at Union City, California and a home for children 1t Covina, California. The Homes are
supported by members of the Masonic Fraternity of California.

20

Method of Accounting:
The financial statements of Masonic Homes of California have been prepared o n the accrual
basis of accounting.

15

Fund Account jng:
Jo insure observance of l im itations and restrictions placed on the use of resources available
to the Homes, the accounts of t he Homes are mainta ined in accordance with the principles of fund
accounting.
The assets, liabilities and fund balances of the Homes are reported in fou r self-balancing
funds, as follow:

10

General Fund - Resources are available to support the operat ions of the Homes at
Union City and Covina, California.
Permanent Endowment Fund - Ordinances of the Grand Lodge provide that no portion
of the principal of the Permanent Endowment Fund shall be upended for any purpose
and income from the principal shall be used only for the maintenance and general
operation of Masonic Homes.

5

Huao M. Lorber Masonjc Home Unjon Cjty Fund - This fund provides for the
operation, prese rvation and betterment of the Home at Un ion City, California.
Restricted Trust Funds - Details to these Trust Funds are contained in Note 9 to the
financial s tatements.

NOTE 7 - LIFE ANNUITY AGREEMENT:

property, entered into an agreement to pay the conveyors during their liretime Sl,250 per month.
The surviving recipient is presently 89 yt>ars old and the liability at June 30 equals the present value

NOTE 8 - HUGO M. LORBER MASONIC HOME, UNION CITY FUND:
From 1982 through 1990 the Masonic Homes of California received bequests from the Estate
of Hugo M. Lorber in the amount of SI 1,983,340. Mr. Lorber's Last Will and Testament provided
that the bequest be used at the Home for the elderly at Union City, California.

The net income from this trust is to be used for higher practical education.
Ayayst F. Heyer Scholarship Fund:
The amount in this fund represents income produced by a trust held by other trustees,
income from which is to be used to provide scholarships to colleges or universities for children of
Masons.
The Charles L. Jacaucljn Annu ity Trus1 Fund;
The principal and income of this fund is held by the Masonic Homes of California subject
to a life annuity.
The Anton Jensen Fund:

The Board of Trustees established the Hugo M. Lorber Masonic Home, Union City Fund
to account for the bequest and resolved that all income from the Fund sho uld be used for operatina,
rehabilitating, preserving and enhancing the Home for Adults at U nion City, as deemed necessary.
The Board of Trustees also rt'solved that the Fund represented a source for additions and
replacements of property at Union City, as represented by t he accumulation of depreciation.
As of June 30, 1989, $12,000,000 had been used to fund construction a t the U nion City
Home.

The principal of this fund, subject to the provision included in the will of the donor, shall
be used for the benefit of the Masonic Home for the Aged.

NOTE 10 - CHANGE IN ACCOUNTING POLICY:

September 13, 1990

Masonic Homes changed its accounting pol icy effective July I, 1989 to reco gnize certain real
estate donated to the organization at current fair market value. (Excluded from this polic y are
vacant lots, for which values are not readily available. See Note I.) Previously all real estate was
valued at a nominal SI value.
The cumulati ve effect of the change in accounting pol icy for periods prior to July I 1989
resulted in an increase to July I, 1989 fund balance of Sl,662,721. The pro-forma effect, h~d the
new method been applied retroactively to earnings for the year ended June 30, 1989, cannot be
dete rmined.

financ ial statements based on our audit.
We conducted our audil in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those standards
require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain r~a~onable assurance about whether t~e fi~ancial
statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes examining. on a test basis. evidence
supporting the amounts and. disclos ures in the financial statements. An audit also include~ assessing the
accounting princ iples used and s ign ifican.t estimates made by man~geme nt, as well as e.v_a luatmg the ov~ rall
financial statement presentation. We believe that our aud it provides a reasonable basis for o ur op1n1on.
In our opinion, the financial s tatements referred to above present fairly, in all material respec!s•
the financial positio n of the Masonic Memo rial Temple at June 30, 1990 and 1989 and the results of its
operations and changes in fund balances for the years the n e nded in conformity with generally accepted
accounting principles.
Our audit was made for the purpose of forming an opinion on 1he bas ic financial statements taken
as a whole. The graphically displayed finan c ial informatio n appearing in Exhibits C and Dis presented
for the purposes of additional analysis and is not a required part <_>f the basic fin.ancial statements. Su~h

Land Buildinu and Eayipment:
Land, buildings and equipment are carried at cost and, except for land, are depreciated on
the straight-line method over estimated useful lives of 50 years fo r Temple buildings, 20 years for
furnishings, five years fo r minor building improvements, and ten years for sound and lighting
equipment. Mainienance and repairs are charged to expense when inc urred . Betterments of a major
nature, which extend the useful lives of buildings and equipment, are capitalized. On sale or
retirement, the cost and accumulated depreciation applicable thereto are eliminated f rom the
accounts a nd the difference between net book value and the proceeds from sale or retirement are
included in income.

NOTE 3 - PENSION PLAN:
The Temple, Grand Lodge and component organizations and Masonic Homes contribute to
the California Masonic Retirement Plan for the benefit of all eligible employees. Details to the plan
are contained in Note 5 to the financial statements of Masonic Homes of California.
Pension expense of the Temple charged to operations in 1990 and 1989 was $21 and S6,S5 I,
respectively.

Collection of Books:
The Temple library contains a book collection of approximately 12,500 volumes. The
collection includes 642 works on Masonic and philosophic topics. Jn 1984, the collection wu
appraised a t a value of approximately $200,000. The Temple expenses books when purchased and
does not recognize donated books as revenue. Accessions and deaccessions of books during 1990
and 1989 were not significant.
The cost of operating the library during 1990 and 1989, including the sa lary of the library
manager, was $28,958 and $26,686, respectively.
Bad Debts:
The direct write- off method is used to recognize uncollectible trade accounts receivable.
Revenye Recognition:
Membership dues are recognized as revenue in the applicable membership period. Jnitiatio1
fees are recorded as revenue in the period the fees are due. Rental revenue is recognized at the
time the physical facilities are used. Contributions are recognized as revenue when received.
Bequests are generally contingent on the occurrence of future events and are, therefore, recorded
as income when received.

NOTE 4 - DESIGNATED RESERVE FOR REPAIRS AND IMPROVEMENTS:
In 1990, the Board of Trustees increased the fund balance appropriated for future major
building repairs and•improvements from $250,000 to $1,000,000. Accordingly, the Temple made
no contributions to Masonic Homes in fiscal years 1990 and 1989.
NOTES - GARAGE OPERATING LEASE:
The Temple is the lessor of the garage premises under an operating lease expiring March 31,
1993. Under t he terms of the lease, the Temple receives minimum monthly rent of $14 ,583. Jn
addition to the minimum monthly rent, the Temple receives a s um equal to 15% of the gross receipts
each calendar month resulting from the parking or garaging of automobiles. Total rents received
in 1990 were $278,910, of which $103,913 were percentage rents on gross revenues. Total rents
received in 1989 were $289,987, of which SI 14,987 were percentage rentals on gross revenues.
Minimum future rentals to be received on the noncancelable garage lease for each of the next

NOTE 6 - FEDERAL EXCISE TAXES:
In accordance with applicable tax provisions, the Temple is classified as a private foundation
and is subject to an excise tax on net investment income, including realized gains. _Accordingly,
federal excise taxes have been recognized in amounts of SI l ,9g6 and SI 1,733 durmg 1990 and
1989, respectively.
Jn addition, the tax provisions require that certain mm1mum exempt program service
distri butions be made in accordance with a specified formula. At June 30, 1990 and 1989, the
Temple had exceeded the required minimum distributions .
NOTE 1 - ADMINISTRATIVE EXPENSES:
Certain administrative costs of the Temple, such as payroll expense of accounting staff, are
provided by the Grand Lodge without charge to the Temple. The value of total administrative
services provided to the Temple without charge for fiscal years 1990 and 1989 has not been
determined.

Board of Trustees
California Masonic Foundation
San Francisco, California

We have audited the accompanying balance sheets of the Cali fo rnia Masonic Foundation, a
California nonprofi t corporation, at June 30, 1990 and 1989, and t he related statements of support,
revenue and expenses and changes in fund balances for the years then ended . These financial statements
are the responsibility of the Foundation's management. Our responsibil ity is to express an opin ion on
these financial statements based on our audit.
We conducted our audit in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those standards
require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial
statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes examining, on a test basis, evidence
supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An audit also incl udes assessing the.
accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management, as we ll as evaluating the overall
financial s tatement presentation. We believe that our aud it provides a reasonable basis for our opinion.
Jn our opinion, t he financial statements referred to above present fairl y, in all material respects,
the financial position of t he California Masonic Foundation at June 30, 1990 and 1989 and t he res ults of
its operations and changes in fund balances for the years then ended in conformi1y with generally accepted
accounting principles.
Our audit was made for the purpose of forming an opinion on the basic financial statements taken
as a whole. The graphically displayed financial informatio n appearing in Exhibits C and Dis presented
for the purposes of additional anal ys is and is not a required part of the basic financ ial statements. Such
information has been subjected to the auditing procedures applied in the audit of the basic financial
statements and, in our opinion, is fairly s tated in all material respec ts in relation to the basic financial
sta1ements taken as a whole.

The California Masonic Foundation was established in 1968 by the Grand Lodge F. & A. M.
of California. The Foundation is formed as a non-profit charitable corporation to further all phases
of education, charity and science.

Scholarship Fund -

NOTE 2 - SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:

This fund was established from a contribution of a variable
appreciable life insurance policy. The policy was redeemed
during 1988. The principal of the fund cannot be expended.
The income of the fund can only be used to fu nd scholarships.

Investments:
Method of Accounting:
The financial statements of California Masonic Foundation have been prepared on the accrual
basis of accounting.

Investments in marketable securities are stated at fair market values. Gains or losses that
result from sales or from market fluctuations are recognized in the period such sales or
fluctuations occur.

Fund Accounting:

Real Estate:

To insure observance of limitations and restrictions placed on the use of resources available
to the Foundation, the accounts of t he Foundation are maintained in accordance with the principles
of fund accounting.

Donated real estate is recorded at t he nominal value of S l pe r parcel for accountability.

support to on-going progr:ims aimed at prevention of drug and alcohol abuse through education of
young c hildren at grade levels 4 through 6. The results of the fund raising effort during the years

In 1990, the Grand Lodge received $370,317 f rom the Estate of Jack I. MacKechnie. Mr.
M3cKechnie's Will provides that the income, but not the principal, shall be used to provide
scholarships to accredited universities and colleges for needy high school graduates of proven
o utstanding athletic abilit y. The Grand Lodge's tax exempt sta tus does not provide for the
grnnting of scholarships to the public at large and at J une 30. 1990 legal proceedings were in
process to transfer the bequest to the Masonic Foundation for administration.
